## [Null-Space Projection Purifies Backdoors in LoRA-Tuned LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00685) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.00685) proposes a backdoor purification method for LoRA-tuned LLMs that uses null-space projection to eliminate backdoors without requiring trigger knowledge, clean reference data, or post-hoc retraining. The method reduces attack success rates from nearly 100% to under 10% while preserving both the base model's general capabilities and the adapter's downstream skills. As LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning becomes the dominant way to customize LLMs, backdoor attacks injected through poisoned adapters pose a serious supply-chain security risk. This method's lack of strong assumptions makes it far more practical for real-world deployment than prior purification techniques that require trigger knowledge or expensive retraining. The approach extracts high-fidelity backdoor directions through careful data curation and feature approximation, then constructs orthogonal null spaces in both input and output channels per layer or head, projecting the LoRA updates onto them. Ablation studies scale the method from a single layer in text classification to full-parameter generative LLMs, though results are from a preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

**Background**: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes a pre-trained model's weights and injects small trainable low-rank matrices into each Transformer layer, drastically reducing the parameters needed for downstream tasks. Backdoor attacks poison training data so that a specific trigger causes malicious behavior at inference time, and such backdoors can persist through fine-tuning. Null-space projection is a mathematical operation that projects vectors onto the orthogonal complement of a subspace, widely used to enforce constraints and prevent interference, such as in continual learning.

## [Robust Nash Alignment Tackles Preference Uncertainty in AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00715) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Robust Nash Alignment, a game-theoretic framework that optimizes a policy for worst-case win rates against an adversarial competitor and any preference kernel within an ambiguity set around a nominal preference. It proposes a four-player primal-dual proxy game with a single-loop optimistic mirror descent-ascent algorithm, proving O(1/√T) convergence and validating it on tabular games and LLM alignment. Current preference-based alignment methods are brittle when pairwise preferences are noisy, heterogeneous, or shift after deployment, which can lead to unsafe or misaligned models. This framework provides a certified lower bound on worst-case performance, offering a principled way to build more robust alignment for LLMs and other AI systems. The proxy game always lower-bounds the truncated hard-constrained objective, and the authors quantify the proxy-to-hard gap and characterize an exactness condition under which the proxy recovers the robust objective. The O(1/√T) average-iteration convergence for the proxy-game duality gap implies a near-optimal robust policy for the original robust objective.

**Background**: Preference-based alignment typically trains a model against a single preference model, assuming pairwise comparisons are reliable. However, real-world preferences can be noisy, heterogeneous across users, or shift after deployment, making the model brittle. Robust optimization addresses this by considering an ambiguity set of possible preferences, and game theory models the interaction between a learner and an adversary. Primal-dual methods are a class of algorithms for solving such constrained optimization problems efficiently.

It also provides a concrete comparison of PPO and GRPO on long-horizon credit assignment, a problem central to reinforcement learning for LLMs. PPO's learned value function can propagate delayed rewards to earlier tokens via generalized advantage estimation, whereas GRPO has no learned value function and assigns a group-relative advantage from complete rollout returns, so it cannot identify which earlier turn caused an outcome and yields zero normalized advantage if all rollouts receive the same return. ## [DARS: Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping for LLM Agent RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01207) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose Dependency-Aware Reward Shaping (DARS), a method that represents task progress as predicates linked by prerequisite relations and assigns step-level credit over the dependency graph. An annotator marks which predicates each step verifies, invalidates, or repairs, and verified predicates are discounted by graph distance from the nearest broken prerequisite while independent predicates remain unaffected. Terminal rewards in reinforcement learning for LLM agents provide little guidance about which steps matter, and existing step-credit methods overlook that work built on uncorrected mistakes is wasted while independent work remains valid. DARS improves success by up to 10 points over GiGPO on ALFWorld and integrates with methods like GiGPO and ARPO/AEPO without changing their rollout strategies or optimizers. DARS uses a fixed potential to convert annotations into signed per-step rewards, and repairs update weights based on remaining errors while invalidated predicates need re-verification to regain credit. Experiments across five task families and models from 1.5B to 8B show gains on ALFWorld, WebShop, Search-R1 QA, and AIME24/25, and a distilled 8B annotator matches the API annotator on ALFWorld.

## [HHR: Hierarchical Hash Retrieval Speeds Up Long-Context LLM Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01230) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01230) proposes Hierarchical Hash Retrieval (HHR), a coarse-to-fine framework that combines Geometry-Aware Key Routing (GKR) and Learned Hash Projection (LHP) to fix the mismatch between Hamming distance and attention relevance in hash-based sparse attention. On LongBench, HHR raises the average score by 1.10 points and, at 128K context length, delivers up to 3.30x decoding speedup and 2.83x end-to-end speedup for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with code released on GitHub. Long-context inference is one of the biggest computational bottlenecks for LLMs, and hash-based retrieval is an attractive way to cut attention cost, but its accuracy loss has limited adoption. By aligning Hamming distance with true Query-Key relevance ranking, HHR makes hash-based sparse attention more faithful, which could make very long contexts (128K and beyond) practical for deployment on existing hardware. The core insight is that Query-Key logits depend jointly on directional similarity and feature magnitude, while hash binarization discards magnitude information, causing false-positive retrieval of low-logit keys and false-negative omission of high-logit keys. GKR learns a head-wise orthogonal transformation to redistribute feature magnitudes and derive more discriminative page-level logit bounds for pruning, while LHP learns a head-wise projection space that aligns Hamming distance with true relevance ranking for fine-grained retrieval.

**Background**: As LLM context windows grow, the attention mechanism must compare each query against a rapidly expanding set of keys, which becomes a severe computational bottleneck. Hash-based retrieval addresses this by encoding queries and keys into binary codes and using fast Hamming distance to select only a subset of keys, approximating full attention with sparse attention. However, binary codes lose information, so the keys selected by Hamming distance are not always the ones with the highest attention scores, degrading generation quality.

The framework jointly refines advisor invocation and information use, and experiments on mathematical reasoning and coding tasks show improved performance-cost tradeoffs over existing collaboration baselines. The learned strategy also transfers to other advisor model families without further training, though the paper focuses on black-box API settings and budget-constrained querying.

## [RIAG: Revision-Aware Agent Graphs for Dynamic Task Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01249) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Homogeneous RIAG achieves 54.24% joint routing-and-answer accuracy at 0.62 calls/query, versus 32.22% at 18.00 calls/query for the strongest baseline, while heterogeneous RIAG reaches 49.78% at 0.63 calls/query. This work addresses a real trade-off in multi-agent systems between wasteful recomputation after every event and stale reuse of outdated conclusions, and its large-scale dynamic episode dataset provides a new benchmark for evaluating agent reasoning under revision. It is likely to interest AI/ML and multi-agent systems researchers working on dynamic task routing and efficient agent orchestration. RIAG caches solutions by immutable document identity, starts each fresh task with two unexposed attempts, and conditionally invokes audit and repair, using at most four calls per document version. The benchmark comprises 31,119 dynamic episodes and 373,428 temporally categorized queries derived from six standard datasets.

## [DeFA: Dependency-Guided Failure Attribution for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01256) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DeFA introduces a dependency-guided framework that builds an event dependency graph from protocol relations and semantic dependencies, then traces failure propagation to pinpoint the decisive error, responsible agent, and error category in LLM agent executions. It achieves the highest responsible-agent and exact step accuracy across all evaluated backbones on the Who and When and Who and When Pro benchmarks, and its diagnostic feedback improves downstream task accuracy by 6-15 percentage points in Trace2Skill. Failure attribution is a critical bottleneck for debugging and improving LLM agent systems, where errors and their visible consequences are often separated by many steps. DeFA's ability to localize decisive errors and feed diagnoses back into skill evolution shows that automated failure analysis can directly improve agent reliability on subsequent tasks. To handle long trajectories, DeFA partitions executions into segments and combines the current segment's detailed content with summaries of other segments, giving local diagnosis access to global context. Ablations confirm the contributions of segmentation, the event dependency graph, and the failure propagation graph, and experiments on image and video trajectories demonstrate applicability to multimodal failure attribution.

## [SCOPE-AD: Cost-Aware Sequential Planning for Alzheimer's Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01278) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced SCOPE-AD, a sequential cost-aware planning framework that combines energy-based models with ordinal belief tracking to decide which diagnostic tests to acquire for classifying cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment, and Alzheimer's disease cases. On the ADNI dataset, it achieved 77.70% Macro-F1 at an average acquisition cost of $50.46, beating the strongest baseline by 9.34 percentage points. This work addresses a real clinical pain point: fixed-modality predictors cannot decide which test to order next or when enough evidence has accumulated, leading to unnecessary patient burden and cost. By showing that selective acquisition can match near-full-modality accuracy at a fraction of the cost, it points toward more practical and economical AI-assisted diagnostic workflows. The framework uses a mask-aware ordinal model to represent uncertainty along the ordered CN–MCI–AD continuum, trains an energy-based teacher with sampled Bellman targets from retrospective records, and distills its action distributions into a Qwen policy. Notably, full-modality evaluation only raised Macro-F1 by 1.89 points while increasing acquisition cost by 116.7 times, underscoring the value of selective acquisition.

## [ITC-MoE: Token-Aware Compression for MoE Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01296) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ITC-MoE, an importance-guided token-aware compression framework for Mixture-of-Experts diffusion language models that combines Importance-guided Adaptive Tucker Compression (IATC) with Token-aware Compensation and Routing (TCR). On SDAR-30B-A3B-Chat-b32, it retains 96.33% accuracy on MultiArith under a 30% compression budget while achieving up to a 7.22x end-to-end speedup, with code released on GitHub. MoE diffusion language models offer parallel decoding and high capacity but are expensive to store and run, so a method that cuts costs while preserving generation quality could make these models far more practical to deploy. The work also highlights that redundancy and token utilization in MoE DLMs are non-uniform, which may influence how future efficient-inference and compression research is designed. The framework exploits two observed properties: cross-mode non-uniform redundancy, where sensitivity to rank truncation differs across input, output, and expert modes, and token-wise utilization variation, where hot and cold tokens show distinct spectral characteristics and expert activation patterns. IATC jointly factorizes expert weights across multiple modes and adaptively allocates ranks under a fixed parameter budget, while TCR applies lightweight low-rank compensation to compression-sensitive hot tokens and restricts the candidate expert set for cold tokens.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models split a network into specialized sub-networks called experts, and a gating network routes each token to only a few of them, increasing capacity without proportionally increasing computation. Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text through iterative denoising rather than left-to-right autoregression, enabling flexible parallel decoding. Combining the two yields MoE DLMs with large expert parameter counts, and existing low-rank compression methods typically use static factorization and fixed rank allocation that ignore how redundancy varies across modes and tokens. Tucker decomposition is a tensor factorization technique that can compress multi-dimensional weight tensors into smaller core and factor matrices.

## [TRACE: Token-Level Training for Multi-Turn LLM Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01323) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce TRACE (Trajectory Return Attribution and Contrastive Erasure), a token-level training objective that attributes refusal to specific tokens and contrasts a frozen reference model with its refusal-ablated copy. Across five open-weight models and seven multi-turn attacks, TRACE achieves the lowest attack success rate in all 35 model-attack pairs, while MMLU and HellaSwag utility drops by at most 1.23 points. Multi-turn attacks that spread a harmful goal across individually benign turns are a known blind spot for safety-aligned LLMs, and existing preference objectives that score whole responses cannot control risk on unseen conversation histories. TRACE offers a theoretically grounded, token-level fix that improves multi-turn robustness without meaningfully degrading general model utility, making it valuable for AI safety and alignment researchers. The method derives sufficient conditions under which suppression at supervised single-turn contexts bounds multi-turn trajectory risk, accounting for coverage, transfer slack, and leakage. On safe responses, each token is weighted by the discounted return of a refusal-attributable advantage comparing a frozen reference model with its refusal-ablated copy; at high-gap positions on rejected responses, TRACE combines the observed token with policy-selected alternatives, and a gradient-norm penalty replaces the retain set.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Safety-aligned LLMs often refuse a harmful request when it is asked directly, but may comply once the same goal is spread across several turns of a conversation. Preference-based alignment objectives score entire responses to single prompts, so their training loss alone cannot directly control risk on unseen multi-turn histories. Refusal ablation is a technique that removes a 'refusal direction' from a model's weights, producing a copy that tends to comply rather than refuse; TRACE uses such an ablated copy as a contrastive signal to identify which tokens drive refusal.

## [Evidence-Based Verification Audit for Modular Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01348) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01348) proposes a claim-specific verification audit for modular agents that plan, act, check, and refine, scoring the evidence behind each conclusion rather than the agent's aggregate task score. The audit records each conclusion with its supporting evidence, one of four verdicts (supported, unsupported, unresolved, or not evaluated), and the boundary within which it holds, using oracle policies, component replacement, and a verifier-validity test as its three tools. Aggregate task scores cannot reveal whether improvement was attainable, which component lost value, or what an agent's own checks actually certify, so this evidence-based audit offers a more diagnostic way to assess modular agent systems. It could influence how AI agent pipelines are evaluated, especially in safety-critical or high-stakes deployments where knowing why a component failed matters as much as knowing that it did. Oracle policies measure attainable improvement under an explicitly stated action set, so a low value can be traced to the evaluation rather than the environment, while replacing one component at a time with a perfect counterpart locates lost value, with null results read as unresolved whenever a downstream component could mask them. Applied to a constrained portfolio-allocation agent in a synthetic market with known hidden regimes, the audit found that the value of perfect regime information depends on the action set used to measure it, that the scenario generator discards most of the regime signal, and that the runtime verifier can be bypassed with no visible change in outcomes.

Developers typically judge changes to one component by an aggregate task score, but such scores conflate many factors and cannot attribute value or failure to specific parts. Oracle policies are idealized reference policies used in reinforcement learning to measure attainable performance, and component replacement is an ablation technique that swaps one part for a perfect version to isolate its contribution.

## [RLCPR Fixes Posterior Concentration in Verifier-Free RL for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01458) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.01458) identifies a length-dependent failure mode called the Posterior Concentration Phenomenon (PCP), where probability-based rewards for verifier-free RL collapse into a low-variance interval as reasoning traces grow long. The authors propose RLCPR, a framework combining uncertainty-aware data sampling and concentration-aware regularization, which outperforms the state-of-the-art verifier-free RL baseline by up to 4.0% on six of seven benchmarks while improving token efficiency. Verifier-free RL is a promising path to train LLMs on general reasoning tasks where no external verifier exists, but this work shows its probability-based rewards become unreliable in long-horizon reasoning. By diagnosing PCP and offering a concrete fix, the paper could improve the stability and efficiency of RL training pipelines that rely on GRPO-style optimization, affecting researchers and practitioners building reasoning models without verifiable rewards. The PCP is defined as the probability of a reference answer conditioned on a reasoning trace collapsing to a low-variance interval as the trace lengthens, making rewards nearly indistinguishable under GRPO-based settings. RLCPR addresses this with two components: uncertainty-aware data sampling that reduces concentration-prone rollouts before generation, and concentration-aware regularization that penalizes unnecessarily long traces when posterior rewards collapse.

## [FedLore Shares Low-Rank Basis to Cut Federated Learning Costs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01620) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces FedLore, a federated learning method that shares a single low-rank optimization basis across all clients within each round and refreshes it across rounds. This shared basis enables exact aggregation in low-rank coordinates, eliminates the projection bias caused by independently chosen client subspaces, and allows the accumulated model update to exceed the per-round rank budget. Federated training of foundation models is bottlenecked by client memory and communication costs, and existing LoRA-style low-rank adapters have a fixed rank budget that limits adaptation. FedLore shows that accurate local gradient compression does not automatically preserve global descent, and its shared-basis design could make communication- and memory-efficient federated pre-training more practical. The authors characterize the aggregation bias and prove an O(T^{-1/2}) stationarity bound for the projected-SGD variant under a global-gradient coverage condition, standard smoothness and variance assumptions, and bounded gradient heterogeneity. Experiments on vision and language tasks, including federated pre-training, show FedLore outperforms evaluated low-rank adapter baselines and matches or exceeds full-parameter training while reducing communication and optimizer-state memory.

**Background**: Federated learning is a distributed machine learning setting where multiple clients collaboratively train a model while keeping their data decentralized, and it is complicated by data heterogeneity because client data is often not independently and identically distributed. LoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes pre-trained weights and injects trainable low-rank decomposition matrices, greatly reducing trainable parameters. Gradient low-rank optimization generalizes this idea by compressing gradients into low-rank subspaces, but when each client picks its own subspace, the local projections interact with data heterogeneity and bias the aggregated update direction.

## [Study Measures Error Propagation in Action Chunking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01626) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.01626) empirically injects small action errors at each state and measures how fast they grow or shrink under open-loop (replaying the rest of the chunk) and closed-loop (replanning after perturbation) execution. Across twelve manipulation tasks from three benchmark suites, it finds confidently stable states are rare and error amplification is common, with propagation rates strongly dependent on the fitting horizon. Action chunking is a core technique in modern robot imitation learning (e.g., ACT, diffusion policies), and this work challenges the common assumption that chunking mainly works by reducing error compounding. It suggests closed-loop reactivity should be trained explicitly rather than expected to emerge from standard imitation learning, which could reshape how robot policies are designed and evaluated. The paper labels each state as contracting, expanding, or unresolved based on a fitted propagation rate, and finds amplification is typically front-loaded, so short fitting windows can overestimate longer-horizon propagation. It also trains predictors showing that a state's open-loop regime can be recovered from camera frames and proprioception alone, while closed-loop propagation is only partially recoverable because it depends on how the policy acts after the perturbation.

## [vFedProtoQNAS: Prototype-Guided Personalized Quantum NAS for Virtual Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01718) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.01718) introduces vFedProtoQNAS, a method that lets each client in a quantum federated learning system independently search and train its own device-specific quantum neural network (QNN) without ever aggregating model parameters across clients. Instead of averaging weights, federated collaboration happens through class-wise prototype sharing, where local prototypes are refined using global prototypes from the server as semantic anchors. Experiments show a 3.70% accuracy improvement over FedAvg and better class-consistent representation alignment. This work tackles a core obstacle in quantum federated learning: heterogeneous device capabilities make a single shared QNN architecture unsuitable for all clients, yet averaging parameters across structurally different circuits mixes semantically inconsistent operations. By decoupling architecture personalization from parameter aggregation, it offers a path toward practical, privacy-preserving quantum machine learning on resource-constrained and heterogeneous edge devices. Each client independently performs quantum neural architecture search (QNAS) and training, then computes class-wise local prototypes from latent representations that are refined against global prototypes acting as federated semantic anchors. The reported 3.70% accuracy gain over FedAvg comes with improved class-consistent representation alignment, though the work is a preprint and the abstract does not specify datasets, circuit sizes, or the number of clients evaluated.

## [Quasar: First Model-Free Q-Learning for Reachability in MEC-Free MDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01781) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers Lu-Chin Chang and a co-author present Quasar, the first model-free Q-learning algorithm with asymptotic convergence guarantees for reachability specifications on MDPs that are free of non-terminal maximal end components (MECs). Quasar uses temporal-difference updates to converge to an optimal policy without ever estimating transition probabilities, cutting memory from O(|S|^2|A|) to O(|S||A|) and converging with orders of magnitude fewer samples than prior model-based methods on the Quantitative Verification Benchmark Set. This is a concrete step toward practical deployment of reachability learning and specification-guided reinforcement learning, since dropping the need to learn transition probabilities makes the approach far more memory-efficient and sample-efficient. It matters for researchers working at the intersection of reinforcement learning and formal verification, where reachability is a core specification. The asymptotic guarantee holds only on the fragment of MDPs free of non-terminal MECs, which the authors note is a building block to which every MDP reduces via the standard MEC quotient. The algorithm follows the classical Q-learning approach and was evaluated on the standardized Quantitative Verification Benchmark Set.

## [Component Routing Decides What GUI Agents Learn vs. Retrieve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01787) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01787) introduces component routing, which splits a GUI agent's accumulated experience into four components—locators, procedures, state facts, and lessons—and sends each either into model weights via fine-tuning or into the prompt via retrieval. Tested across three backbone families, two environments, and three seeds, the authors find locators and lessons perform better in the weights while procedures and state facts perform better in context, and a rule based on recurrence and state-conditionality recovers the correct destination in 24 of 24 held-out cells. Prior work disagreed on whether self-improving GUI agents should fine-tune on past trajectories or retrieve them into the prompt, and this paper shows the disagreement stems from treating a trajectory as a single unit. The finding that different experience components belong in different destinations could reshape how agent designers build memory and self-improvement pipelines, and the routing rule beats every whole-trajectory baseline by an average of 3.5 points. The routing rule is fitted using two properties measured before any training—recurrence and state-conditionality—and two interventions are shown to move a component toward the boundary between destinations. The paper also documents that note readout decreases after the same component is written into the weights (most for the most recurrent items), context gains increase with the information gap, and weights gains decrease with the policy gap; code and data are promised for release.

LineupRL introduces a reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) pipeline for time series captioning in which the reward signal is caption-to-series identification: a frozen LLM verifier reads the generated caption and candidate time series as raw numeric values (never as charts) and must pick the described series from multiple distractors. It also shows that a 3B vision language model trained by LineupRL outperforms, at 1/24 of the parameters, the 72B VLM whose captions the SFT baseline is distilled from, suggesting a more scalable path for time series understanding and multimodal learning. The verifier is an off-the-shelf frozen LLM that never sees the chart, only raw values, because matching a caption to a series is a far lighter demand than writing questions or judging caption quality. The paper's case study shows LineupRL resists reward hacking, and that the trained captioner both traces the trend and names the values at key points.

A new arXiv preprint (2610.01842) proposes a formalization and benchmark for time series world models (TSWMs), introducing a metric called mechanism consistency that tests whether shifting an action moves forecasts in the declared direction, such as a vasopressor raising blood pressure. Across eight public datasets, seven backbones, and five seeds, the authors find that the lowest-error configuration is at or below chance in consistency on four of five datasets with declared mechanisms, and that a directional supervision loss can raise consistency without changing MAE. This work exposes a critical gap in how world models are evaluated: a model can be an accurate forecaster yet fail to respond correctly to unexecuted plans, which is precisely what world models are meant to do. It matters for AI/ML and systems research because it suggests that prediction error alone is an insufficient evaluation criterion, and it offers concrete design guidance (frozen latent space, output-side fusion, directional supervision) for building more trustworthy planners and controllers. The benchmark consolidates eight public datasets with real actions from engineered infrastructure and clinical care, varying prediction space, plan fusion, and plan encoding. A frozen latent prediction space lowers MAE by 9.9% over observation space and gated output fusion lowers it by 12.7% over input concatenation on average, while temporal plan encoding changes average MAE by at most 2.2%; notably, no design choice avoids the accuracy–consistency divergence.

## [Zero-Knowledge Verification of Oracle-Aided AI Is Impossible Without Signed Oracles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01995) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01995) proves that, in the random oracle model, there are no zero-knowledge proofs for all oracle-aided computations, even when both prover and verifier run much longer than the computation itself, and this impossibility extends to the debate model for scalable oversight. On the positive side, the authors show that if the oracle cryptographically signs each of its answers, every oracle-aided computation can be verified in zero knowledge with an efficient prover and verifier, assuming only collision-resistant hash functions. This result draws a sharp theoretical boundary for privacy-preserving AI verification: without signed oracle responses, zero-knowledge verification of AI outputs that depend on confidential data or external oracles is fundamentally unattainable. It also offers a new scalable-oversight path that avoids relying on an honest opponent (as in debate) or on the robustness of the computation (as in prior single-prover protocols), which matters for AI safety and cryptographic protocol design. The impossibility holds in the random oracle model and covers debate, a canonical model for scalable oversight, while the positive construction requires only collision-resistant hash functions and achieves an efficient prover and verifier. The paper thus shifts the focus from efficient verification (which is impossible for general oracle-aided computation) to privacy, allowing the verifier to run in time polynomial in the computation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Zero-knowledge proofs are cryptographic protocols in which a prover convinces a verifier that a statement is true without revealing anything beyond that truth; they can be interactive or non-interactive. Oracle-aided computation models settings where correctness depends on an external oracle such as human judgment, a physical experiment, or the web, and prior work studied verifying such AI outputs via interactive proofs and debate with a fast verifier. This paper instead asks whether those interactive arguments can be zero knowledge when the verifier is allowed to run in time polynomial in the computation, so that the verifier learns nothing about the confidential data beyond the correctness of the output.

## [Mimir: Physics-Grounded LLM Agents for Long-Horizon Irrigation Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02038) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02038) introduces Mimir, a physics-grounded LLM agent organized around two repair timescales for long-horizon irrigation control. Under a common retrospective evaluator across multiple sites, crops, and years, Mimir achieves the lowest reported aggregate control cost among evaluated references and uses about 51% less irrigation than historical schedule replay. Most evidence for LLM agents comes from episodic tasks with immediate feedback and reset failures, whereas long-running physical control involves compounding errors and immutable physical rules. Mimir shows that persistent physical agents can combine semantic reasoning with bounded, evidence-driven self-improvement while reserving physical truth and actuator authority for explicit numerical mechanisms, which could influence how LLM agents are deployed in agriculture and other safety-critical physical systems. At the fast timescale, a structured physical interface and deterministic simulator turn an LLM output into a proposal that is numerically checked, revised, and subject to bounded deterministic action selection before execution; at the slow timescale, recurrent failure patterns are consolidated into persistent contextual principles while the physical model, evaluator, and execution constraints remain immutable. Ablation studies show higher control cost when forward simulation, verified revision, or persistent context is removed, and model-scale and model-family studies show no monotonic gain from increasing LLM size.

## [HydroJEV: One-Second, Training-Free Triage for Water Network Alarms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02048) ⭐️ 7.0/10

HydroJEV introduces Jev, a training-free model that returns class probabilities in about one second for attributing SCADA alarms in water distribution networks to cyberattacks, physical faults, normal transients, or faulty sensors. On a four-class benchmark built on the C-Town network in EPANET, Jev matched a hand-written rule tree (macro-F1 0.62-0.64 vs 0.56-0.61) and exceeded a supervised classifier by 0.36-0.42 on event subtypes absent from its labels across four sealed, pre-registered rounds. Utilities rarely have labelled incident data and frontier LLMs take tens of seconds per decision, so a fast, training-free screen could take over about a third of the review load in SCADA anomaly triage while preserving the accuracy of deliberate review. This matters for critical infrastructure security, where operators must quickly distinguish cyberattacks from routine faults. With only a label-free prior correction, Jev decided 20-40 times faster than frontier LLMs, and accepting only benign Jev verdicts confirmed by the rule tree spared an LLM reviewer 35-38% of windows on fresh sealed sets without loss of macro-F1. Transferred unchanged to two further networks, the gated cascade stayed within the non-inferiority margin of its reviewer on all four sets.

## [Causal Memory Policy Makes Memory Utility Identifiable by Intervening on Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02070) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Causal Memory Policy (CMP), a causal framework that intervenes on retrieval itself by reserving a fixed number of context slots for memories sampled with known propensities, thereby restoring identification of memory utility in memory-augmented LLMs. It proves the causal factorization of memory utility through retrieval, the unbiasedness and exact variance of a self-normalized inverse propensity weighting estimator, and the optimal decision rule under irreversible operations, while empirically showing that identification fails for 54% of required memories on LongMemEval and 67% on LoCoMo. This work addresses a fundamental positivity violation in memory-augmented LLMs, where memories that are never retrieved cannot have their utility estimated, and it shows that identified memory utility alone is insufficient for retention decisions because per-query utility reaches 0.78 AUC on the query for which it is estimated yet no aggregation predicts a memory's value on unseen queries. The theoretical guarantees and optimal decision rule could influence how future memory systems decide which memories to retain, affecting the design of long-context and lifelong-learning LLM applications. CMP uses a balanced assignment design with self-normalized inverse propensity weighting to estimate memory utility, and the paper reports that identification failure persists in a deployed memory system, with CMP improving discrimination between required and non-required memories from 0.54 to 0.66 AUC. The code is available at an anonymous repository, and the work is a preprint without community discussion or engagement metrics.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Memory-augmented large language models store external memories and retrieve relevant ones to condition on long contexts, but deciding which memories to retain requires estimating each memory's effect on task performance. Causal inference relies on the positivity assumption, which requires that every treatment level has a nonzero probability of being observed within each covariate stratum; when a memory is never retrieved, store-level interventions produce identical outcomes, creating a retrieval-level positivity violation. Inverse propensity weighting is a statistical technique that reweights observed data by the inverse probability of treatment to estimate causal effects under non-random treatment assignment.

## [Homomorphic Advantage Operator Stabilizes FHE-Based Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02074) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02074) introduces the Homomorphic Advantage Operator (HAO), a stabilization framework that prevents polynomial approximation divergence in fully homomorphic encryption (FHE)-based deep reinforcement learning. HAO adapts zero-mean centering from advantage-based value estimation directly to temporal-difference (TD) targets, eliminating the uniform state-value baseline that drives the recursive error phenomenon known as Bellman drift. This work addresses a critical barrier to deploying privacy-preserving reinforcement learning on cloud systems handling confidential data, where FHE enables computation on encrypted data but non-linear operations must be replaced by polynomial approximations. By strictly bounding network pre-activations within the safe polynomial approximation domain, HAO could make encrypted RL practical for sensitive applications such as healthcare or logistics without expensive ciphertext bootstrapping. HAO requires zero additional non-linear multiplicative depth and avoids expensive ciphertext bootstrapping; in experiments across a tabular MDP, an encrypted CartPole environment using real CKKS cryptographic operations, and a 20-node logistics routing benchmark, HAO agents achieved 0% boundary breaches across all random seeds, versus 3 of 5 seeds for regularization alone and 83.8% of episodes for the unstabilized baseline. HAO also improved optimal policy accuracy by 18.0 percentage points in tabular domains and remained stable when DP-SGD-style Gaussian noise was added to clipped gradients.

**Background**: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) allows computations to be performed directly on encrypted data without decryption, preserving confidentiality in cloud environments. In RL, temporal-difference updates are recursive, and approximation errors can accumulate and diverge—a phenomenon the paper calls Bellman drift.

The paper finds a length-191 snake in dimension n=9, improving the previous record of 190 that had stood for 14 years, and establishes new lower bounds in dimensions 10-13. It introduces snakepits (collections of disjoint snakes) to expand the search space, a new Snakepit-in-the-Box benchmark, and Beam Anchor, a search-supervised learned constructor that finds 100 inequivalent length-190 snakes in dimension 9. The Snakepit-in-the-Box benchmark shifts the objective to maximizing edge counts when multiple disjoint components are allowed, and Beam Anchor demonstrates that learned constructors can generate many inequivalent near-optimal solutions.

STATERA adapts a pretrained V-JEPA video backbone with mostly frozen weights and a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame center-of-mass (CoM) heatmaps and trajectories from short monocular videos of opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer the authors observe a fundamental supervision trade-off: phase-aware targets can induce bimodal predictions, while phase-agnostic targets can collapse toward statistically safe centroids. Their phase-aware STATERA-50K-Crescent is the only evaluated method that consistently moves toward the true hidden offset, improving physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%, though it exhibits a monocular vector overshoot artifact that marginally increases absolute Euclidean error relative to a static geometric centroid.

## [First-Token Logit Readout Overstates LLM Judge Position Bias](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00054) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.00054) shows that reading an LLM judge's verdict from the first generated token's logits systematically overstates position bias, because judges often do not lead with a verdict token. Across three Qwen3 judges, this non-commitment occurs on 12% to 49% of pairs, and forcing a read on those pairs returns whichever response was shown first rather than an actual judgment. This matters because constrained decoding and likelihood-scoring evaluation harnesses commonly use first-token logit readout as a cheap, generation-free way to obtain judge verdicts, so reported position-bias figures from such setups may be inflated upper bounds. The distortion moves position bias by 42 points while moving judge accuracy by under one point in seven of ten conditions, meaning it misleads auditors of judges rather than users. Pooled over the 924 pairs where a judge did not commit, the forced read flips on 89.7% of them when responses are swapped, versus 47.5% when read after generation (paired difference +0.422, 95% CI [+0.365, +0.467]). A second, smaller failure occurs even when the judge does lead with a verdict token, since it sometimes opens with one letter and reasons its way to the other, on 0 to 5.5% of pairs at a rate uncorrelated with compliance.

**Background**: LLM-as-a-judge is a common technique where a language model evaluates and compares candidate responses, often used to score model outputs at scale. Position bias is the tendency of a judge to prefer responses based on their ordinal position rather than quality, and it is typically measured by swapping response order. Constrained decoding and likelihood-scoring harnesses can obtain a verdict by reading the logits of the first generated token, avoiding full generation, but this paper shows that shortcut distorts the measurement.

## [Billing-aware CPU TTS serving on serverless cuts costs 4.1x](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00063) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.00063) introduces billing-aware neural TTS serving on serverless CPUs, combining request-sized concurrent inference with a reclaimable instance lifecycle. On the Kokoro-82M model, the system reaches 2.71 audio-seconds per CPU-second versus 0.89 with ONNX Runtime defaults, and cuts cost per audio-hour from $0.0631 (PyTorch) to $0.0153, a 4.1x reduction. Instance-billed serverless platforms charge for CPU and memory over a warm instance's lifetime, so idle inference state becomes a direct serving cost that conventional runtimes ignore. The approach bounds per-request CPU parallelism to avoid contention under concurrency and releases inference state and page-cache memory after idle periods while retaining the server process and compile cache. Idle billed memory drops from 8.7 GB to 1.33 GB, and restoration to first audio takes 2.2 s versus 7.7 s for a PyTorch cold start; under bursty traffic, lifecycle reclamation is essential for turning inference efficiency into lower serverless cost.

## [Survey Proposes SAVER Framework for Self-Evolving Agent Safety](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00093) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv survey (2610.00093) examines safety challenges in self-evolving LLM agents and introduces SAVER, a transition-centered framework built on five components: Substrate, Adaptation, Violation, Exposure, and Response. The authors coded 683 papers and argue that safety must be evaluated longitudinally, tracing unsafe influence back to its originating transition and verifying repair across descendant states. As LLM agents begin to update their own memories, tools, skills, and even parameters after deployment, safety can no longer be treated as a one-time alignment check on a single response. This survey reframes the problem for the AI safety and agent research communities, warning that legitimate experience accumulated in one context can become unsafe when reused with greater persistence, authority, or scope. The survey finds comparatively strong evidence for admission, retrieval, activation, exposure, and local containment, but much less for descendant repair and evaluation after adaptation resumes. It emphasizes that failures need not originate from harmful information, since legitimate state can become unsafe when adaptation expands its persistence, authority, or scope beyond the conditions under which it was valid.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Self-evolving LLM agents are systems that continue to change themselves after deployment, refining prompts, memories, tool definitions, skills, workflows, and sometimes model weights from their own experience and feedback. Unlike standard LLMs whose parameters stay fixed after training, these agents accumulate reusable state, which turns past interactions into potential future causes. SAVER is a framework that organizes this safety problem around transitions: where reusable influence lives, how it changes, what safety attribute is compromised, where failures become observable, and how they can be contained, repaired, or revoked.

## [Nous: Learning Memory Decisions Can Beat Source Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00094) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.00094) proves that on a four-model hidden Markov family, learning an unknown Bayes decision requires Theta(l^-2) records and certifying its improvement takes O(l^-2) fresh records, while fixed-precision source estimation requires Theta(l^-4) as persistence l vanishes. The authors also introduce a finite-sample certificate using observable witness regions and validate it on 45,000 held-out mutable-state histories plus 9,000 episodes across three MiniGrid memory environments. This result separates decision learning and certification from source calibration, showing that agents may not need to recover source reliability before acting well — a distinction with direct implications for memory-augmented agents operating on noisy, copied, or stale evidence. It offers theoretical grounding for when memory decisions can be justified cheaply, which matters for researchers in AI/ML theory and agent memory design. The sharp identified interval for policy improvement is characterized under an unknown identity-plus-background report channel, and the certificate uses observable witness regions without pure-class anchors; a robustness extension tolerates bounded history-dependent misspecification and conditional copying. In MiniGrid tests the new certificate accepts 9/9 improvements over a constant incumbent and 4/9 over last-write-wins, whereas the earlier certificate accepts none, though strong established inference baselines remain competitive or better.

## [Verifier Leakage Can Make Agent Debugging Comparisons Vacuous](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00126) ⭐️ 7.0/10

This finding matters because agent developers increasingly rely on simulator-grounded verifiers to compare prompts, tools, policies, and diagnosis algorithms, and a verifier that encodes the target identity can make solver comparisons meaningless. It argues for replacing solver-first evaluation with a support-gated verification contract that checks evidence eligibility and non-revelation before optimizing the component selector. In a preregistered heldout of 1,440 cases and 21,600 partition rows, 55/72 regime-component units passed the reference gate, 54/55 passed the runtime gate, and stable false admission was 0/20 represented components with a one-sided exact 95% upper bound of 0.1391; within admitted units, affected clean traffic predicted detection better than nominal fault-cell fraction.

## [Neuromodulation Alone Fails Parity Tasks; Activation Selection Solves Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00148) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A large-scale study of over 10,000 experiments on indirectly encoded substrates evolved via CPPNs shows that neuromodulation alone hits a 75% ceiling on parity tasks, regardless of capacity, topology, or population size. Combining neuromodulation with per-task activation function selection (oscillatory for parity, monotonic for threshold tasks) achieves 100% simultaneous 5-task success across all 30 seeds, with a median of 14 generations. This work identifies a fundamental evolutionary search barrier rather than a representational limit, since Adam gradient descent reaches 100% on the identical architecture. It suggests that for open-ended artificial life, the computational primitive itself should be an evolvable trait, guiding future neuroevolution research toward co-evolving activation functions. The barrier extends to higher-arity and asymmetric tasks, while adding multi-layer depth offers an alternative path to solving them. The result generalizes across the oscillatory activation class, with all four tested functions reaching 100% success across 30 seeds each, and neither mechanism suffices alone.

## [Paper Proves a Natural Way to Deepen Soft Decision Trees Cannot Learn](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00180) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.00180) analyzes four ways to grow constructive classifiers and proves that the most natural method for deepening a soft decision tree—turning each leaf into a gate whose two children inherit the parent's class distribution—produces identically zero gradients for every new gate, so the added level can never learn. The author proposes a fix: a small random perturbation of the children, whose size barely matters, and recommends asserting nonzero gradients after adding parameters. This gives an exact theoretical diagnosis of a fundamental failure mode in constructive classifiers, distinguishing it from known issues like the symmetry Net2Net breaks with noise or the saddle point that splitting steepest descent escapes with second-order information—here first-order information is not weak but absent. It could directly influence how practitioners design and grow tree-structured and constructive models, and the proposed one-line test is a cheap safeguard for any parameter-adding procedure. Over three seeds of five-fold cross-validation, the function-preserving construction loses 19.6 accuracy points on Iris, 19.1 on Wine and 55.6 on Digits compared with the same depth trained from scratch, and with the gate at 1/2 the two children receive identical gradients. Of the other three growth decisions, fitting a new hidden unit to the residual error buys a smaller network on every dataset (though not a more accurate one, and it significantly costs accuracy on Digits), splitting the leaf with the largest expected error buys sparsity (0.885 with 3.7 splits versus 63 for a complete depth-six tree, but loses 4.3 points on a harder problem), and requiring statistical significance before a more expressive split buys nothing.

## [CAVE-Mem Validates Experience Applicability via Boundary Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00238) ⭐️ 7.0/10

CAVE-Mem introduces a training-free framework that represents past search experience as a typed intervention operator with applicability, boundary, and utility conditions, rather than relying on relevance alone. It first obtains a base memory-search answer, then permits an operator to modify it only if the operator matches the current substrate, answer contract, evidence boundary, and cross-fitted utility; otherwise the system abstains. Current experience-memory systems optimize relevance and inject similar past lessons into prompts, but a relevant experience can still be harmful when the memory substrate, question intent, answer granularity, or evidence boundary changes. By adding boundary-aware validation, CAVE-Mem could make memory-augmented agents safer and more reliable for long-horizon personal, factual, and narrative reasoning tasks. The framework is training-free and uses cross-fitted utility to decide whether an experience operator should be applied, abstaining when conditions are not met. Experiments across long-term conversational memory, multi-hop question answering, and long-document narrative reasoning reportedly show consistent gains over relevance-only experience reuse.

The paper distinguishes two prediction targets—identifying questions a model is likely to answer correctly versus distinguishing correct from incorrect responses to the same question—and shows that certainty's predictive value depends on the target, the model, the certainty metric, and which token positions are aggregated. The practical method allocates the number of responses using early-generation certainty and weights answer votes using late-generation certainty.

The paper introduces Locket (LoRA-Oriented Control via Keyed Entry Tokens), a framework that trains multiple lightweight LoRA adapters, each encoding a distinct access policy such as full reveal, PII redaction, or differential-privacy-level reveal. A compact gating module performs sequence-level hard routing to associate a learned keyed entry token with exactly one adapter, so a valid token unlocks private knowledge while an invalid or absent token triggers a privacy-preserving redaction adapter. This addresses a critical privacy gap in LLM deployment for healthcare, finance, and government, where models can memorize and leak personally identifiable information. By embedding policy-driven access control directly into generation while remaining compatible with off-the-shelf LLMs, Locket offers a practical path to regulatory compliance without sacrificing model utility or fine-tuned private knowledge. Locket was evaluated on Enron, ECHR, and Yelp datasets across Qwen3 (1.7B and 8B), Llama-3.2 (1B and 3B), and Gemma-2-2B; with the correct token it preserves perplexity comparable to fine-tuning on raw data, while a missing or invalid token substantially reduces PII leakage at utility and perplexity on par with strong baselines. Adapter routing selects which LoRA adapter to apply for a given query, and differential privacy is a mathematical framework ensuring a model's behavior is approximately the same whether or not any individual training example was included. Each receipt contains an emission anchor that deterministically locates the claim inside a committed answer or claim-bearing action, plus source identifiers, offsets, hashes, quotes, and a domain-separated execution commitment. The design separates an integrity plane from a pluggable support plane so structural validity is not treated as a proxy for entailment; on an independently adjudicated 384-pair split, the conflict-aware support guard reached F1 0.8865 with 0.0729 false acceptance, and 0.8679 F1 with 0.0938 false acceptance on unseen failure families.

## [Worst-Case Constrained RL Improves LLM Reasoning Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00332) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.00332) formulates LLM reasoning distillation as a constrained reinforcement learning problem, where the task reward is maximized subject to a worst-case constraint on teacher log-likelihood along every prefix of the student's chain-of-thought. The authors derive an unaugmented constrained MDP with a low-variance policy gradient decomposition that provably satisfies the worst-case constraint almost surely in the penalty limit, and report the highest rigorous Reasoning Success Rate across mathematical reasoning and code generation benchmarks. Current distillation methods face a tension between reward hacking under pure RL objectives like GRPO and diluted task performance under soft KL-based regularization, which can let students mask severe logical errors with high teacher agreement elsewhere. By enforcing a worst-case rather than average constraint, this work expands the accuracy-fidelity Pareto front and could make distilled small models more trustworthy for efficient deployment in reasoning-heavy applications. The method avoids the prohibitive cost of dual Lagrangian solvers and the test-time teacher dependence of state-augmented approaches such as Saute by transforming the reward while preserving hard-constraint semantics. Experiments show it matches the high Final Answer Correctness of pure RL while drastically reducing teacher constraint violations, though the constraint is only guaranteed almost surely in the penalty limit.

**Background**: Knowledge distillation transfers the reasoning ability of a large teacher LLM into a smaller student model, typically by training the student to imitate the teacher's token probabilities using KL divergence. Constrained reinforcement learning, as in worst-case soft actor-critic (WCSAC), maximizes reward subject to safety constraints, and this paper adapts that idea to reasoning chains where validity depends on the weakest step.

A staged reservation freezes predecessor residual authority during replacement, a partitioning fork validates the complete child family, and each commit atomically fences the predecessor and activates successors; an independent checker accepts all 64 original traces and rejects 28/28 semantic mutants.

PGS prevented all 50 drift scenarios from producing attacker gain, and the only unprevented family—an in-policy drain—was bounded by a per-session budget; overhead is about 41k gas and 0.1–0.2 seconds per check. ## [GNNs Learn Local Set Cover Under Hard Information Horizon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00422) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper formalizes combinatorial optimization under a hard information horizon as local set cover, proving that any deterministic selector with a horizon one hop short must fail coverage or be a factor Δ from optimal, and that an L-layer GNN read out at the deciding node is exactly an L-hop selector. The authors instantiate this on weighted MPR selection in OLSRv2 (RFC 7181), where a 3-layer GATv2 with a coverage-completing decoder, behavior-cloned from CP-SAT, reaches cost/opt = 1.030 ± 0.001 versus greedy's 1.138, closing 79.1% of the gap at 100% coverage. This work shows that the information horizon, not model capacity, is the dominant variable in distributed combinatorial optimization, with implications for GNN expressiveness theory and for practical protocol design in mobile ad hoc networks. It also provides a rare theoretical bridge between neural combinatorial optimization and the hard constraints of real routing protocols like OLSRv2. The paper proves that at the horizon, a GNN of depth O(Δ) reproduces the RFC 7181 covering greedy, and at width O(c_max Δ) its metric-aware weighted analogue, both inheriting the (1+ln Δ_2)-approximation. Empirically, restricting the same learner to one hop collapses performance to 1.344, far worse than greedy, and on 40,308 instances of real battalion mobility the frozen model closes 48% of the gap at full coverage.

The paper introduces Random Recursive Models (RRM), which maintain a pool of L learned layers and perform T recursive steps by independently sampling one layer with replacement for each example and step. On challenging reasoning tasks, RRM matches or exceeds baselines while often using 50-75% fewer parameters, and it can vary inference depth beyond training depth without retraining or adding parameters. This work suggests a new architecture design direction where parameter count is decoupled from computational depth, potentially enabling more efficient reasoning models and flexible test-time compute scaling. It could benefit researchers and practitioners building compact models that need deep iterative computation without proportional parameter growth. RRM supports Monte Carlo inference and probabilistic test-time scaling, both of which improve performance without retraining. The approach retains the parameter efficiency of recurrence while allowing flexible layer reuse, though results are from a preprint and lack community discussion so far.

## [No Single Red Team Architecture Wins Across Cyber Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00557) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.00557) presents a controlled cross-environment comparison of two homogeneous hierarchical red team architectures — an RL planner with an RL executor (RL+RL) and an LLM planner with an LLM executor (LLM+LLM) — evaluated against expert autonomous defenders in CybORG CAGE-4 and Cyberwheel at two network scales across 18 configurations. The study finds a pronounced environment-dependent inversion: RL+RL dominates CAGE-4 (78.5% vs. 18.0% disruption success) and the 100-host Cyberwheel network (81.0% vs. 50.5%), while a pretrained cybersecurity LLM agent wins the larger 1010-host Cyberwheel network (55.0% vs. 0.0% for RL). The results show that conclusions drawn from a single environment may not generalize, warning researchers and practitioners against assuming one decision mechanism is universally superior for autonomous red teaming. This has direct implications for how hybrid planner-executor designs should be motivated — by specific failure modes rather than architectural preference — and for the broader development of AI-enabled cyber defense and offense. A kill-chain analysis explains the inversion through architecture-specific bottlenecks that aggregate success rates conceal: in the 1010-host Cyberwheel network, RL discovers and compromises hosts but stalls at privilege escalation, whereas in CAGE-4, LLM agents obtain privileged access but rarely convert it into operational impact. All evaluations use one unified disruption metric, and the paper is a preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

## [SLIDER Uses Partial Information Decomposition to Evaluate LLM Reasoning Quality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00571) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces SLIDER, an interpretability framework that applies Partial Information Decomposition (PID) to disentangle the information about the final answer between two consecutive reasoning steps into unique, redundant, and synergistic components. Building on this decomposition, the authors propose the Step-wise Repetitive Reasoning Index (Step-RRI), which improves step-level redundancy identification accuracy by over 10 points on the redundancy class of the PRMBench dataset compared to embedding-similarity and information-gain baselines. Large reasoning models often generate lengthy, repetitive, or erroneous reasoning trajectories, and SLIDER offers a theoretically grounded way to quantify this repetitiveness, which could help diagnose reasoning failures and improve reasoning efficiency. The framework's Trajectory-RRI measure correlates strongly with actual reasoning length across QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and GPT-4.1, suggesting practical value for model evaluation and training data selection. The paper defines Trajectory-RRI as an aggregate measure of repetitiveness for an individual reasoning trajectory, and demonstrates that Trajectory-RRI-guided data selection for fine-tuning can improve a fine-tuned model's reasoning efficiency while largely preserving task performance. As an arXiv preprint, the work has not yet undergone peer review, and its evaluation focuses on the redundancy class of PRMBench and three specific models.

Testing six models from 3B to 70B parameters across small, medium, and large networks, the authors find that a frozen general-purpose 70B model holds successful lateral movement to roughly 1% of steps and attacker impact near zero across all three network scales using the same weights, while the RL baseline must be retrained for each scale. Replacing only the planner with an LLM yields limited gains as network size increases, whereas extending LLM control to execution produces notable improvements for sufficiently capable models, indicating that strong tactical execution is essential to realizing the benefits of LLM-based control.

## [ALER: Adaptive Learnable Experience Rewriting for RL Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00592) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce ALER (Adaptive Learnable Experience Rewriting), an agent that pairs an LSTM with a slot memory, using an independently addressed Gumbel-Softmax write to overwrite a single slot and a learned gate to fuse retrieved content with the recurrent state. They also formalize two new memory requirements—rewriting and experience fusion—and release Rune-Mazes, three environments where rune observations invert, cancel, reset, or repeat updates of a hidden cue. ALER reaches at least 0.82 success across all sixteen Endless T-Maze configurations and at least 0.99 on all five Rune T-Maze compositions, beating seven baselines. Most RL memory architectures and benchmarks only test retention—keeping information unchanged until needed—so this work exposes a real gap in how agents handle obsolete or transformed memories in partially observable settings. By formalizing rewriting and experience fusion and providing concrete environments and a working architecture, it gives RL researchers a new benchmark and design pattern for memory systems that must actively update stored experience. The Gumbel-Softmax write concentrates weight on one slot to perform a hard overwrite, while a learned gate controls fusion of retrieved content with the recurrent state before the policy and value heads. The paper counts the memory states a solution needs and shows several baselines hit their lowest success rates on compositions requiring more states; ALER also outperforms PPO-LSTM on pixel-based Rune MiniGrid Memory in eight of ten configurations.

A new arXiv paper (2610.00619) reports that two independent proximal policy optimization (PPO) agents playing a finite-horizon Almgren-Chriss liquidation game achieve trading costs below the Nash benchmark, and identifies a learned punitive mechanism: when one agent deviates by imposing a profitable off-equilibrium trade, the opponent accelerates liquidation, more than offsetting the deviator's gain in every run and both player roles while leaving the punisher's own average payoff materially unchanged. This provides behavioral and economic evidence that deep reinforcement learning agents can autonomously converge on tacit collusion in market microstructure settings, raising concerns about algorithmic collusion if such agents are deployed for real-world trade execution, and offering a formal test for distinguishing genuine punishment from coincidental behavior. The authors formalize two checks — whether punishment outweighs the gain from deviating, and whether the change in trading behavior is large enough to account for the loss imposed — and both hold for the tested deviation; matching deviations and subsequent additional selling rise and later decline during training, yet final policies retain an effective punitive response even though more profitable, less punitive liquidation plans are available.

StepRS-GRPO offers a theoretically grounded, drop-in modification to the existing GRPO trainer that could make RL fine-tuning of dLLMs more effective for reasoning tasks. For binary rewards, the authors prove the transformation is exactly a prompt- and state-dependent rescaling of centered outcome advantages, and a capability-based calibration suggests the coefficient scale. Ablations with mass-matched controls and RMS-matched advantages support the contributions of state allocation and schedule direction, and reasoning-trace diagnostics show diversity gains extend beyond final-answer strings.

**Background**: Diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text by iteratively denoising a sequence or successive blocks, revealing several tokens in parallel rather than strictly left-to-right like autoregressive models. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) is an RL algorithm that scores a group of sampled answers per prompt and rewards answers that beat the group average, popularized by DeepSeekMath and DeepSeek-R1. RLVR (reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards) uses automatically checkable outcomes, such as a correct final answer, as the training signal. Pass@1 measures whether a single sample is correct, while pass@k measures whether at least one of k samples is correct.

Researchers introduced VisionQ, the first benchmark built from peer-reviewed CVPR and ICCV comparison figures that grounds every VLM judgment in a named visual criterion. It includes 1,409 papers, 1,800+ validated figures, 3,911 hand-annotated data points, a six-axis 51-leaf taxonomy, a criterion-conditioned evaluation protocol, and VisionQ-Judge, a DPO-tuned Gemma-4-E4B judge that improves accuracy by 2.5pp and cuts last-option predictions by 7.0pp. Existing VLM-as-a-Judge benchmarks only score scalar quality or overall preference, so a model can be rewarded for choosing the right image for the wrong visual reason. VisionQ addresses this gap by forcing judges to justify choices against author-stated criteria, which could make automated evaluation of computer vision papers more trustworthy and expose reliability differences across criteria. Evaluating 20 open- and closed-source VLM judges, the strongest model reaches only 63.1% accuracy against a 32.2% chance baseline, and reliability varies sharply across criteria. The evaluation protocol hides method names, captions, and paper identity to prevent shortcut learning, and VisionQ-Judge is trained on symmetric evidence pairs to reduce positional bias.

## [Total Variation, Not KL Divergence, Predicts Decision Flips in Compressed LMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00694) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.00694) shows that total variation, not KL divergence, directly predicts the rate at which a compressed language model's arg-max token changes (the flip rate). Across 802 compressed and perturbed copies of 19 open models on five corpora and nine perturbation families, the flip rate tracked total variation at a median ratio of 1.05 with no fitted constant. This gives deployment engineers a concrete, calibration-free metric for estimating how many decisions a compressed model will change relative to its dense counterpart, which matters for reliability reporting and for techniques like speculative decoding. It also suggests that current compression reports relying on KL divergence can misrank compressors in about 11% of cases. KL divergence converts into flip rates only through its square root and a factor that varies fourfold across models and corpora, because KL averages over tokens before the root is taken; first-order per-token statistics such as Hellinger distance avoid this but are rarely reported. In vLLM speculative decoding, total variation measured under teacher forcing predicts greedy draft acceptance with a mean relative error of 1.1–2.4%, without task-specific calibration.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Model compression techniques such as quantization and pruning produce smaller, faster language models, but these compressed models may make different predictions than the original dense model. KL divergence is the standard way to report how far a compressed model has drifted, but it measures distributional distance rather than the practical question of how often the model's top choice (arg-max token) changes. Total variation distance is another statistical distance between probability distributions, defined as half the absolute area between their curves, and it directly captures the probability mass that differs between two distributions.

## [FTC: Sequential Tucker Compression for LLM Attention Without Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00717) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.00717) introduces FTC, a sequential structured compression framework for LLM attention that adapts each approximation to the already-compressed model while jointly exploiting the native Q/K/V head structure under a fixed storage budget. Across seven decoder-only LLMs from 6B to 32B parameters, FTC achieves the lowest WikiText-2 perplexity among compared methods at every tested keep ratio on five modern GQA models, with the largest gains under aggressive compression, and requires neither fine-tuning nor gradient-based recovery. LLM attention projections dominate parameter count and inference memory, so a post-training compression method that needs no fine-tuning and still beats existing baselines could substantially lower the cost of deploying large models. The gains persisting at the 32B scale and transferring to downstream tasks suggest the approach may be practically useful for efficient inference in real deployments. FTC formulates compression as a sequential process rather than independent matrix approximation, handling the output projection separately to account for the changed post-attention representation, and it operates under a fixed storage budget. Evaluation covers seven decoder-only models from 6B to 32B parameters, with the largest improvements under aggressive compression, though the work is a preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Tucker decomposition is a tensor factorization that decomposes a tensor into a small core tensor and a set of factor matrices, generalizing matrix SVD to higher-order data; it is widely used to compress multi-dimensional structures. In transformer attention, each token is projected into Query, Key, and Value (Q/K/V) matrices, and multi-head attention runs several such projections in parallel so different heads can capture different relationships. Grouped Query Attention (GQA) reduces memory by sharing Key and Value heads across groups of Query heads, and is used in many modern LLMs. Post-training compression aims to shrink these attention weights after training, typically without retraining the model.

## [Verbalized and Internal Probabilities Are Coupled in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00827) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.00827) systematically intervenes on the underlying uncertainty sources in training and in-context data to test whether large language models' internal sampling probabilities align with their verbalized confidence statements. The authors find that both readouts are shaped by distributional and asserted uncertainty in training data, and that verbalized and internal probabilities are aligned beyond what independent tracking of the same uncertainty sources would predict. This matters because it suggests verbalized confidence can serve as a probe of a model's internal distribution, which is directly relevant to calibration, hallucination detection, and trustworthy AI. If verbalized uncertainty reliably reflects internal probabilities, downstream systems and agents could use stated confidence for safer decision-making. The study uses an intervention-based approach, manipulating distributional versus asserted uncertainty in the data rather than only observing naturally occurring alignment. The key caveat is that alignment is demonstrated under controlled interventions, so it remains to be tested how robustly this coupling holds across different model families, scales, and real-world prompting conditions.

**Background**: Large language models implicitly assign probabilities to the tokens they generate, which can be read out as an internal notion of uncertainty. ## [SHARPO Brings Segment-Level Credit Assignment to Agentic RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00838) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SHARPO (Segment-level Hindsight Advantage Reweighting for Policy Optimization) refines GRPO by computing teacher-student log-probability gaps within each environment-facing segment and using them to derive a bounded multiplier on the GRPO advantage. With Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, it outperforms GRPO, SDAR, RLSD, and StepOPSD on the ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks. Credit assignment is a core bottleneck in agentic RL, where a single localized error can cause task failure and trajectory-level rewards give little guidance for individual decisions. A lightweight, bounded reweighting of GRPO could improve multi-step agent training without adding a critic model, benefiting the broader LLM agent and RL communities. SHARPO is inspired by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) and shares a single bounded multiplier across all tokens within a segment, so credit can vary across segments while remaining stable. It is evaluated only with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct on ALFWorld and WebShop, so generalization to other models, tasks, and scales remains to be shown.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a critic-free RL algorithm popularized by DeepSeekMath and DeepSeek-R1: for each prompt it samples a group of outputs, scores them, and rewards answers that beat the group average. Agentic RL trains an LLM to act over long, multi-step interactions with an environment, such as text-based household tasks in ALFWorld or e-commerce navigation in WebShop. Because GRPO assigns the same trajectory-level advantage to every token, it cannot tell which intermediate decisions were actually responsible for success or failure.
