A new arXiv paper (2610.00840) introduces token-wise incremental trajectories of contextual word embeddings, recomputing a token's embedding as each successive word is added to a sentence to capture how meaning evolves in transformer LLMs such as RoBERTa. Using garden-path sentences as a test case, the authors show these trajectory metrics reliably distinguish garden-path sentences from matched disambiguated controls and reproduce known processing disruption around the critical region. This work offers a new framework for studying utterance-specific meaning construction in LLMs, bridging NLP interpretability and cognitive modeling of human sentence processing. It also suggests that utterance-level information is distributed across multiple representational scales, not just the sentence-level CLS vector, which could influence how researchers probe and interpret transformer representations. The authors introduce several metrics for quantifying representational displacement across contextual increments, and find that ambiguity-related information is recoverable not only from the CLS representation but also from ordinary vocabulary tokens. Exploratory analyses show qualitatively similar trajectory structures in other ambiguity- and misdirection-related linguistic phenomena, though the abstract is truncated and full experimental details remain to be verified.

## [Kinematic MeanFlow Enables One-Step Action Generation for Robot Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00864) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce Kinematic MeanFlow (K-MF), a one-step action generation policy for Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) that decouples the time derivative in the MeanFlow formulation using a kinematic identity to avoid performance collapse. K-MF reduces action-head latency of GR00T-N1.6 by 67.5%–74.4% on L40 and Jetson Orin, yielding end-to-end latency reductions of 30.3%–54.9%. High inference latency from multi-step flow matching is a major bottleneck for deploying robotic foundation models in real-time control, and K-MF's one-step generation could make such models practical on edge devices like Jetson Orin. The approach also outperforms multi-step flow matching in most settings, suggesting a path to both faster and better action policies. The performance collapse of vanilla MeanFlow in RFMs is attributed to two dynamics in the velocity field: local acceleration surges sharply near the end of denoising, and the spread of its magnitudes across samples widens as denoising progresses. K-MF decouples the time derivative into two sub-interval terms separated by an intermediate point, capturing early- and late-stage denoising dynamics while mitigating error amplification; code will be available at https://github.com/IntelChina-AI/K-MF.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Robotic Foundation Models (RFMs) are large vision-language-action models that generate robot actions, often using flow matching—a generative modeling technique that learns a velocity field to transport noise to data over multiple denoising steps. MeanFlow is a recent framework that introduces an average velocity field to enable one-step generation, achieving strong results in image generation. However, directly applying MeanFlow to RFMs causes performance collapse, which this paper addresses with a kinematic decoupling of the time derivative.

The framework combines isolated workspaces, Lean tools, and fresh review with statement comparison, axiom audits, and independent proof checking where supported. A new arXiv paper (2610.00888) shows that a lightweight post-training pass on a frozen Qwen3-8B reasoning model, using only about 2.5B tokens of target-generated chain-of-thought with plain cross-entropy, can match or exceed the expected throughput speedup of jointly pretrained MiMo-7B MTP heads on math, coding, and knowledge benchmarks. The authors report using 10^3–10^4 times fewer MTP-training tokens than joint pretraining, and they introduce a chain-aware relaxation of draft-token verification that lifts expected speedups by 12–16% per benchmark, plus an adaptive controller that recovers 11–14% of lost speedup. This work suggests that the expensive joint pretraining currently used by every open MTP release (MiMo-7B, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3) may be unnecessary, potentially allowing any frozen reasoning model to gain MTP throughput speedups through a cheap post-training pass. If validated, it could substantially lower the cost of deploying speculative-style multi-token drafting in serving systems. The recipe uses K=3 chained MTP heads on a frozen Qwen3-8B and relies on target-generated chain-of-thought rather than the original pretraining corpus; the proposed verification relaxation permits a bounded drift from the backbone token distribution while preserving task accuracy. The adaptive controller dynamically selects how many MTP heads to engage at inference, addressing the loss that occurs when a fixed maximum draft length is used.

TOAST diversifies the discrete supervision while preserving the underlying robot action, and the gains grow as training data decreases, though results are limited to LIBERO and four real-robot tasks.

## [LLMs Address Facts by Order of Mention, Not Entity Names](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00910) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.00910) introduces the "ordinal addressing hypothesis," showing that large language models represent which fact a question asks about by the fact's order of mention in context rather than by the entity names it contains. The authors identify a steering vector called the "ordinal vector" that, when added to a question about the first fact in a new list, makes the model answer with the second fact instead. This finding suggests LLMs internally organize contextual facts by position rather than by entity identity, which could reshape how researchers interpret model reasoning and how practitioners design prompts and retrieval-augmented contexts. It also offers a mechanistic handle for steering model outputs toward specific facts, with implications for interpretability and controllability. Across Qwen, Gemma, and Llama, the fact addresses are ordered by mention, steerable, low-rank (with the first-mentioned fact easiest to reach, resembling human recall), and emergent—shared in late-middle layers, stable from 1.5B to 32B parameters, and formed early in pretraining. The work is a preprint without peer review, so its conclusions remain to be independently verified.

A new arXiv paper introduces GUI-HARVEST, an automatic harness optimizer that lets GUI agents self-improve without fine-tuning their backbone models. It aligns model outputs and executed actions with before-and-after screenshots, treats repeated runs of the same task as a joint evidence unit, and consolidates verified findings into bounded source-code edits; on OSWorld-Verified, Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct gains 12.33 points, and frozen-harness transfer improves GPT-5 by 13.87 percentage points on WindowsAgentArena at 50 steps. This work shows that substantial GUI-agent performance gains can come from optimizing the executable harness rather than retraining the underlying model, which lowers the cost of improving agents and makes the approach applicable to proprietary models. It also outperforms Self-Harness and Meta-Harness with the same backbone and initial harness, suggesting GUI-specific diagnosis and validation help harness improvements generalize to unseen tasks. The method records predicted behavioral effects before evaluation and checks them alongside task performance through repeated execution, promoting or rolling back each edit with fixed score and behavior gates. Experiments cover six general-purpose open, GUI-specialized open, and proprietary backbone models, and the code is available on GitHub.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: GUI agents are AI systems that operate graphical user interfaces by taking screenshots as observations and emitting actions such as clicks and keystrokes. The executable harness around a GUI model determines how observations are assembled, actions are executed, and verification, recovery, and termination are controlled. A frozen backbone is a pre-trained base model whose parameters are kept fixed, so adaptation happens through external components rather than weight updates. Automatically optimizing a GUI harness is harder than for non-GUI agents because it must reconcile model intent with observed visual effects, diagnose failures under variable execution outcomes, and turn recurring failure patterns into reusable runtime changes.

## [SaCRL: Structure-Agnostic Causal Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00968) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduce SaCRL, a framework that jointly identifies causal structure and learns invariant representations without requiring prior structural knowledge, formulating structure selection as a soft optimization over candidate invariances using HSIC-based violation metrics with adaptive weights. The paper provides theoretical guarantees for structure identification, invariance satisfaction, and out-of-distribution generalization, and reports state-of-the-art accuracy on three DomainBed benchmarks (PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome) plus strong results on Colored MNIST and Bayesian-network benchmarks. Existing causal representation learning methods require specifying the causal structure a priori, and misspecification causes representations to discard predictive information; SaCRL removes this bottleneck, potentially making causal representation learning more practical for real-world settings where the true structure is unknown. Its strong out-of-distribution generalization results could benefit domains like medical imaging and autonomous driving where distribution shifts are common. The method uses HSIC-based violation metrics to softly select among candidate invariances, with adaptive weights that concentrate on the achievable structure, and it degrades gracefully under structural misspecification and limited environment diversity. Theoretical guarantees cover structure identification including under random-feature approximation, invariance satisfaction, and out-of-distribution generalization; code is available at https://github.com/ArmanBehnam/sacrl.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Causal representation learning (CRL) is a machine learning subfield that aims to learn high-level causal variables and their cause-effect relationships from low-level observations such as images or text, rather than merely fitting correlations. Traditional CRL methods assume the causal structure is known in advance, but different structures impose incompatible invariance constraints, so a wrong assumption harms predictive performance. Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization refers to a model's ability to perform well on test data whose distribution differs from the training data, a key challenge in real-world deployment. HSIC (Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion) is a statistical measure of dependence between random variables often used to test and enforce invariance constraints.

## [RelationVGGT: Feed-Forward, Pose-Free 3D Spatial Relation Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00970) ⭐️ 7.0/10

RelationVGGT introduces a new task called 3D spatial relation segmentation, where a model receives a visually specified subject and a relational text query and must segment the target object across multiple views without ever being told the target's category name. The framework combines semantic features from a visual foundation model with geometry-aware representations from a 3D geometry foundation model (VGGT-style) and uses a relation transformer for subject-conditioned, cross-view relation prediction, requiring neither per-scene optimization nor known camera poses. This work pushes 3D scene understanding beyond object-centric perception toward relational reasoning, which is essential for applications like robotics, embodied AI, and augmented reality where an agent must find an object described by its relationship to something else (e.g., 'the cup on the table'). By making the pipeline feed-forward and pose-free, it lowers the deployment barrier compared to per-scene optimization methods that require known camera poses. The method operates in a multi-view setting and predicts the target across views without receiving its category name, relying instead on the visually specified subject and the relational text query. The authors also provide a fully automated annotation pipeline built on ScanNet++ using VLMs and LLMs to generate scalable training data for this new task.

## [Divide-and-Remember: Recursive Memory for Long-Horizon VLA Policies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00982) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Divide-and-Remember (D&R), a recursive memory method for vision-language-action (VLA) models that formulates what to remember as an optimization problem. It derives an objective that maximizes the conditional mutual information I(a_t; m_t | o_t) between the action and memory given the current observation, and implements it via a recursive top-K selection over 2K tokens with a shared lightweight selector, achieving state-of-the-art average success on the RoboMME benchmark of 16 long-horizon manipulation tasks under a 64-token budget. Long-horizon manipulation tasks are a major bottleneck for VLA models, and existing memory designs rely on hand-crafted heuristics that yield inconsistent gains. By providing a principled information-theoretic objective and a compute-light recursive implementation, D&R could improve reliability of robot policies in partially observable, history-dependent settings and influence how future VLA architectures handle memory. The method divides full-history selection recursively into subproblems of top-K selection over 2K tokens, so fixed-size selectors learned end-to-end support an unbounded history, and all recursion blocks share one selector to capture a common selection rule. It achieves consistent gains across all four RoboMME suites and in real-robot experiments, though the work is a preprint without peer review or community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are multimodal foundation models that take an image observation and a text instruction and directly output low-level robot actions, typically built by fine-tuning a vision-language model on robot trajectory data. Many real-world manipulation tasks are partially observable, meaning the current observation alone does not determine the correct action, so the policy needs memory of past history; this is naturally modeled as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). Conditional mutual information measures how much information one variable provides about another given a third, and here it is used to define which historical information is action-relevant beyond the current observation.

## [Directional Label Distillation Improves Knowledge Transfer for Asymmetric Relations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00997) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces directional label distillation, where frozen teacher models score candidate answers in the direction they know rather than the requested direction, and the best-scoring candidate becomes the student's training target. On parent-child facts, students trained on known-direction labels improved open-ended accuracy by 13 to 15 points over those trained on prior-corrected reverse labels. This approach addresses a fundamental limitation in knowledge distillation where teacher models fail to generate answers in reverse directions for asymmetric relations, potentially improving how smaller models are trained for efficient deployment. The method could benefit anyone using knowledge distillation to compress large language models, especially for tasks involving directional or asymmetric factual knowledge. The paper demonstrates that with prior-corrected scores, the better direction depends on the facts rather than the template, and reverses on mined facts where the notable entity is the parent rather than the child. Students reproduce nearly all selected labels after generated answers are matched to a fixed name list by lexical similarity, and the label advantage holds on unscreened queries and when candidates are retrieved without inserting correct answers.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Knowledge distillation is a model compression technique where a smaller 'student' model is trained to replicate the behavior of a larger 'teacher' model, enabling efficient deployment on less powerful hardware. Asymmetric relations in knowledge graphs are relations where the direction matters, such as 'parent of' versus 'child of', and teacher models may know one direction but not the reverse. This paper addresses the problem that distilling from a teacher's generated answers can propagate its directional limitations to the student.

## [Weak Reviewers Can Audit Strong Coding Agents With Structured Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01023) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01023) studies when nominally weaker reviewers can reliably audit stronger coding agents, analyzing 411 execution-labeled traces from three agents plus 101 controlled cases. It finds that structured, frozen evidence formats improve defect detection for five of six reviewers on held-out traces, and that reviewer model size is not a consistent predictor of review quality. This matters for AI safety and oversight because it suggests that reliable auditing of powerful coding agents may not require equally powerful reviewers, potentially lowering the cost and complexity of deployment-time oversight. It also highlights that the main bottleneck is producing decisive checks without access to official tests, which is directly relevant to real-world agent deployment. On 154 GPT-5.4 traces, structured but unchecked evidence raised both defect catch and over-rejection; providing official execution evidence served as an upper-bound diagnostic. A frozen cascade using patch-caused static errors and generated tests achieved coverage of 0.89/0.86, risk of 0.33/0.26, catch of 0.76/0.80, and over-rejection of 0.66/0.67 on 121 GPT-5.4 and 59 Gemini held-out traces, with most false rejections occurring when unresolved cases reached the reviewer.

The method requires no additional models, labels, or executions, and DataWright further hardens datasets because workflows are commonly trained and evaluated on data a single agent can already handle.

## [Source-Space MCMC via Few-Step MeanFlow Transport Maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01034) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces a source-space generalized Bayesian inference framework that represents an implicit prior with a one- or few-step improved MeanFlow (iMF) transport map and performs posterior sampling in its Gaussian source space. It establishes Wasserstein error bounds between exact and learned posteriors, decomposed into training suboptimality and model-class approximation error, and adopts parallel tempering with preconditioned Crank-Nicolson updates plus a hybrid split Hamiltonian Monte Carlo variant. This work bridges Bayesian inference with implicit priors and modern generative modeling, offering a principled way to perform posterior sampling when the prior is only available as samples, such as historical ensembles, simulator outputs, or pretrained generative models. It could benefit test-time guidance and generalized Bayes tasks, including CLIP-guided image generation, by providing both practical sampling algorithms and theoretical guarantees. The Wasserstein error bounds are expressed in terms of the joint population iMF and auxiliary-velocity loss, separating training suboptimality from model-class approximation error. Synthetic experiments show accurate and efficient posterior approximation, while CLIP-guided ImageNet experiments demonstrate steering a pretrained iMF image prior toward text-specified preferences.

**Background**: MeanFlow is a one-step generative modeling framework that learns interval-averaged velocity from noise to data, enabling fast, high-fidelity outputs. Parallel tempering, also known as replica exchange MCMC, is a simulation method that improves the dynamic properties of Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, often used for multimodal distributions. A new arXiv preprint (2610.01054) introduces Task Operator (TO), a method that shows each attention head's output is an affine transformation of its context-masked counterpart, with parameters that are empirically stable across samples for a given task. TO replays this transformation as an analytically derived update to the attention output projection, enabling efficient in-context learning (ICL) inference without processing full demonstration sets. By narrowing the gap between zero-shot inference and full ICL, TO could make ICL more practical for real-world applications and stimulate further research into efficient inference and interpretability. The extracted knowledge concentrates in a task-specific sparse circuit across layers and positions, and averaging operators from disjoint demonstration batches enables effective many-shot scaling without expanding the context window. The code is available at https://github.com/gzxiong/task_operator, and the method is evaluated across lexical, algorithmic, and reasoning tasks.

## [MOMAT: Low-Power Jailbreak Defense for Quantized LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01058) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present MOMAT (Mixture of Multiple Atlases), a hardware-enhanced safety framework that defends quantized large language models (qLLMs) against jailbreak attacks by combining multiple semantic atlases with a lightweight Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) detector and a Compute-in-Memory (CiM)-accelerated similarity engine. The CiM-based retrieval accelerates a 100-query batch from 15,052.44 ms to 3,207.21 ns (a 4.69×10^6× speedup) and cuts energy from 8.1×10^7 μJ to 3.32 μJ, roughly a 2.5×10^5× reduction over a DRAM-based Raspberry Pi baseline, while matching state-of-the-art defense performance without benign overkill. Quantized LLMs are increasingly deployed on edge devices for low latency and energy efficiency, but quantization weakens alignment safeguards and makes them highly vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. MOMAT shows that CiM-based modular defenses can make edge-deployed qLLMs both safer and more energy-efficient, which matters for the growing ecosystem of on-device AI security. Each atlas represents a semantic cluster of harmful or benign sample sets and policy templates, enabling domain-localized Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) guarding that mitigates the curse of dimensionality and semantic sparsity in large heterogeneous safety databases. MOMAT retrieves top-k similarity features from all atlases per prompt and evaluates them with a lightweight MoE detector, and the authors plan to release a full 223.2k-sample dataset to foster future research.

Researchers introduce JoinGR, a join-aware table retrieval method that treats the database join graph as the retrieval space, representing columns as graph nodes and intra-table and foreign-key relationships as typed edges. Given a question, JoinGR selects semantically similar anchor tables, traverses join edges with a query-conditioned scorer, and aggregates edge deposits into table scores; it is competitive with the strongest retrieval baselines on BIRD and Spider and substantially improves recall on the multi-hop BEAVER enterprise benchmark. Table retrieval is a prerequisite for Text-to-SQL over realistic databases, and dense retrievers that rank schema elements independently miss tables that are never mentioned in the question but are reachable only through join relationships. The scorer is a lightweight MLP built on top of frozen query, node, and edge embeddings, trained with a pairwise margin loss over gold tables, and cross-domain experiments show the learned scorer transfers across benchmarks, suggesting it captures reusable join-graph traversal behavior. However, the abstract reports only competitive rather than state-of-the-art results on BIRD and Spider, with the largest gains concentrated on the harder BEAVER benchmark.

## [JEV-IDS: System One Model Beats LLMs for Zero-Day Intrusion Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01079) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces JEV-IDS, an open experimental network intrusion detection system built on the Jev System One Model (SOM) that detects zero-day intrusions under label scarcity. On a 300-flow NSL-KDD pilot split, JEV achieved an F1-Score of 0.859, precision 0.941, recall 0.790, and novel-attack recall 0.838, while being 4.8 times faster and 3.8 times cheaper than GPT-5.6 Luna with 1.5 times higher novel-attack recall. Zero-day attack detection under label scarcity is a critical open challenge in cybersecurity, and this work suggests that specialized System One decision models can outperform both large language models and traditional machine learning baselines in speed, cost, and novel-attack recall. If validated at scale, this approach could make practical, low-latency network intrusion detection more accessible to organizations without large labeled datasets. JEV-IDS serializes one flow per request and asks JEV two questions: a binary attack probability and a finite-choice traffic category. Increasing k to 2 reduced its F1-Score to 0.839, and the results are based on a small 300-flow pilot split with 5,400 decisions, so the findings are preliminary rather than a large-scale validation.

OrbitTAMP introduces a hierarchical framework that grounds pretrained LLM reasoning in a graph of reusable behaviors and domain-specific planners for spacecraft task-and-motion planning (TAMP). ## [Madeleine Learns Involuntary Recall for Conversational Memory Without LLM Calls](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01118) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.01118) introduces Madeleine, a method that learns "amortized association" for conversational memory by training a query encoder on cue-trigger pairs generated by an LLM life simulator, so that no LLM calls are needed at inference time. On the LoCoMo-Plus benchmark under the official protocol, Madeleine reaches 66.6 when plugged into HyperMem (the highest among evaluated systems), matches HyperMem's released score of 52.9 with 52.4 when used alone at zero LLM calls and roughly 1/21 of the answer context, and lifts T-Mem by 26.2 points. Long-term conversational assistants currently spend hundreds to over a thousand LLM calls per memory bank and thousands of context tokens per query just to recover relevant memories, so a method that eliminates LLM calls at inference while matching or beating existing systems could substantially cut cost and latency for production memory systems. Because Madeleine only replaces the query encoder, it can plug into any vector memory backend, making it broadly applicable to the growing ecosystem of LLM memory tools. Madeleine treats association as a learnable relevance signal, defined as the pointwise mutual information of memories under how human lives unfold, and trains a residual association on top of frozen similarity using simulated lives. The paper reports that it significantly outperforms the same untrained backbone inside both HyperMem and T-Mem, and leaves ordinary QA intact on the 4B backbone, though it remains a preprint without community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Long-term conversational memory systems must retrieve the right past detail at the right moment, but the most relevant memory is often semantically dissimilar to the user's current utterance — a phenomenon LoCoMo-Plus calls "cue-trigger semantic disconnect." Existing approaches handle this by having an LLM reason at write or read time, which is expensive. Pointwise mutual information (PMI) is a classic information-theoretic measure of association that compares how often two events co-occur versus what chance would predict, and "amortized" here means paying the learning cost once offline so that inference becomes cheap.

## [SURGE Fuses RL Checkpoints to Scale Policies Without Extra Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01133) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01133) introduces policy-space scaling and SURGE (Scaling Up RL Gradient-free via Eigenspace fusion), a method that combines two checkpoints from a single RL run—a high-accuracy anchor and a shorter-response donor—by spectrally decomposing the anchor's update to retain its dominant component while incorporating the donor's complementary component. Evaluated on two 1.5B math-reasoning histories (DeepSeek, Nemotron) and one 7B coding history (OLMo), SURGE improves benchmark-average accuracy over both input checkpoints while using fewer reasoning tokens, reaching 54.17% on DeepSeek AIME24 versus a measured native maximum of 50.83% and 83.7% on OLMo HumanEval+ versus 82.8%. This work suggests that a completed RL training history is a reusable scaling resource, meaning the capability available from a training run need not end at its best checkpoint, which could change how practitioners scale RL for reasoning tasks without spending more training or inference compute. If validated, it offers a cheaper alternative to simply extending RL training or increasing per-query inference computation. SURGE expresses both checkpoints as changes from their shared initialization, then spectrally decomposes the anchor's update; with a fixed target for how much of the anchor update to retain, it determines the block size directly from the weights without testing candidate policies, and each constructed model runs as a single policy. Geometric controls support the importance of RL-update structure beyond weight displacement or token reduction alone, though the results come from an arXiv preprint without community validation yet.

**Background**: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a training paradigm in which a model learns by exploring actions and receiving rewards, and in recent large language model work it has become a key way to improve reasoning abilities. Scaling reasoning typically means spending more compute either on RL training or on inference, and checkpoints are intermediate saved states of a model during training. Spectral decomposition (eigendecomposition) is a mathematical technique that breaks a matrix into simpler components based on its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, which SURGE uses to separate the dominant and complementary parts of a policy update.

## [DR-TFM: Parameter-Efficient Robust Adaptation for Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01143) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose DR-TFM, a parameter-efficient distributionally robust adaptation framework that makes tabular foundation models (TFMs) robust to subpopulation shift without requiring true group annotations. For TabPFN-3, DR-TFM updates only 0.016% of the pretrained model's parameters by fine-tuning or adding a query scaling network that adjusts attention to labeled context examples, achieving substantially higher average worst-group accuracy across five tabular benchmarks while maintaining competitive mean group accuracy. Subpopulation shift is a common and damaging failure mode in real-world deployment, where underrepresented groups suffer large accuracy drops, and existing robust methods like Group-DRO typically require expensive group annotations. DR-TFM shows that strong worst-group robustness can be obtained with negligible parameter updates and no group labels, which is valuable for practitioners applying tabular foundation models in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and income prediction. DR-TFM keeps all pretrained parameters frozen except for a query scaling network, and it is instantiated with two robust objectives based on estimated groups or source conditional distributions derived from training data. The method improves average worst-group accuracy on ACS Income and across four additional TFMs, though it relies on estimated rather than true group information, which may limit robustness in some shift scenarios.

**Background**: Tabular foundation models such as TabPFN-3 are pretrained models that perform strong in-context learning on tabular data, but they can still fail on underrepresented subgroups when group proportions change between training and deployment, a phenomenon known as subpopulation shift. Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) aims to minimize the worst-case loss over subgroups, but classic methods like Group-DRO require group annotations for every training point, which are often unavailable. ## [When Is Deletion Ordering Tractable? A Permutation-Structure Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01149) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01149) studies the permutation objective induced by sequential deletion policies in machine unlearning, identifying two independent reductions—position additivity and suffix localization—that simplify optimization. Under shared affine updates, the authors characterize the quadratic interactions obstructing additivity and show that suffix-conditioned assignment improves the approximation rate from O(p^L) to O(p^(2L)). As machine unlearning becomes critical for privacy compliance and model maintenance, understanding when deletion order affects the final model—and when it can be optimized efficiently—has direct implications for designing scalable unlearning systems. This work provides a rigorous theoretical foundation for ordering deletion requests, potentially reducing the prohibitive cost of retraining after each request. The paper proves the independence of the two reductions and shows that stronger contraction in a damped-Newton sweep shifts the objective toward shorter, more suffix-specific dependence. Experiments recover both structures in executed objectives, and structures identified from compact execution sets predict unseen orders, while two full-network policies exhibit distinct positional and within-suffix structure.

This paper studies the resulting permutation optimization problem, asking when the objective admits simpler structure that enables efficient algorithms.

## [LOOM Enables Looped Mixture-of-Experts LLMs to Scale to 9-12 Loops](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01153) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01153) introduces LOOM, a scalable recipe that overcomes two obstacles preventing looped Mixture-of-Experts LLMs from scaling beyond two loops: hidden-state variance growth and expert selection collapse. Experiments on 100M-1.7B models show stable scaling to 9-12 loops, with the 1.7B model trained on 60B tokens peaking at 9 loops and reducing perplexity from 9.62 to 7.77 while improving average zero-shot accuracy from 42.4% to 47.7%. This work could unlock recurrent depth as a practical scaling axis for large MoE LLMs, allowing models to gain effective depth without increasing parameter count, which matters for compute-efficient training and inference. It also provides a concrete diagnosis and remedy for routing collapse, a known failure mode in sparse expert models. LOOM stabilizes recurrence by scaling residual updates to bound variance growth and re-injecting the input embedding at every loop, while diversifying computation through per-loop routers that engage different experts and a Looping Residual that carries earlier outputs forward. Under near-iso-FLOP conditions, the 700M model performs best at 5 loops, reducing perplexity from 18.36 to 16.54 and improving average zero-shot accuracy from 38.84% to 39.53% over the non-looped baseline; code is available at https://github.com/hed-ucas/LOOM.

The analysis separates approximation, coupling-replacement, nuisance-estimation, generalization, and Monte Carlo errors, and the authors establish finite-sample non-parametric guarantees for the learned velocity and score fields when both the conditional outcome model and the source-target coupling are estimated from data. ## [Audit Finds 4B VLM Judge Barely Beats Random on Image Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01243) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01243) audits vision-language models acting as judges for image selection on 300 culturally situated prompts, comparing their returned images against unseen human ratings and random choice while reordering candidates. The 4B-parameter judge barely beats random and falls short of a CLIP similarity baseline, picking the first image in 49% of calls (chance: 28%) and changing its choice on 60% of prompts when reordered, while an 8B judge shows almost no position bias and outperforms CLIP. This matters because VLM judges increasingly decide which generated images users see, yet they are typically validated only by score agreement with human ratings rather than by the images they actually return. The findings show that agreement-based filters can discard good decisions or keep wrong ones depending on the judge, so any such filter must be re-audited whenever the judge changes. For the 4B judge, decisions that survive reordering are much better than random, but agreement with a weaker second judge keeps the wrong ones; for the 8B judge, the same filter mostly discards good decisions. The 4B judge's slight rise in stereotype ratings is no longer detectable after aggregating across orders or when using the larger judge.

## [PROMO: Preference-Conditioned Multi-Objective RL for Quadruped Robots](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01260) ⭐️ 7.0/10

In simulation, 67 of 100 sampled preferences produced non-dominated behaviors under exact Pareto dominance with a mean preference-objective correlation of 0.843, and the same policy transferred zero-shot to a Unitree Go2, where preference changes alone reduced specific energy by up to 30.4%, position error by 38.7%, and peak body-attitude deviation by 59.0%. It could simplify how legged robots are tuned for missions that prioritize speed, stability, or battery life, and it points toward more flexible, preference-driven control across robotics. PROMO separates deployment-facing preferences from embodiment-specific locomotion priors, keeping the reward shaping terms needed for viable gaits fixed while making the trade-off an explicit runtime input. The evaluation covers 100 sampled preferences in simulation and a zero-shot transfer to a Unitree Go2, with open-source code and videos available at the project page.

## [PickMoment unifies deblurring and blur-to-video in one continuous-time model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01279) ⭐️ 7.0/10

PickMoment introduces a continuous-time reformulation that directly learns the interval-mean blur over arbitrary sub-intervals of the exposure window using a single deterministic network, trained with three supervisions derived from the blur integral: an empirical reconstruction loss, an additivity loss enforcing self-consistency across overlapping sub-intervals, and a sharp-frame loss anchored at the zero-interval limit. A single trained model unifies single-image deblurring, blur-to-video generation, and continuous-time pick-a-moment recovery as different queries to the same network, achieving state-of-the-art results among generative-based deblurring methods on GoPro and HIDE and the highest per-frame fidelity on GoPro-7 blur-to-video in a single forward pass. This work reframes motion blur according to its physical definition—temporal integration of a sharp signal over an exposure window—rather than sidestepping it, potentially offering a more principled foundation for both image restoration and video generation from a single blurred input. By unifying deblurring and blur-to-video in one deterministic model without iterative sampling, it could simplify pipelines for photographers, video editors, and downstream vision systems that must recover motion from blurry captures. The model draws an analogy to MeanFlow's average-velocity formulation, learning interval-mean blur instead of instantaneous quantities, and requires no separate training for each task. It achieves these results in a single forward pass without iterative sampling, though the paper notes it is competitive rather than dominant against restoration-based methods on RealBlur.

**Background**: Motion blur occurs when a camera's shutter stays open for a finite exposure time, integrating a continuously changing scene into a single smeared image. MeanFlow is a recent generative modeling technique that learns average velocity fields over time intervals to enable high-quality one-step sampling, and PickMoment adapts this interval-averaging idea to the blur integral.

A new arXiv paper by Hanna Malet and Gabriel Turinici studies feature-selective model collapse in diffusion models, comparing a total replacement protocol (training only on synthetic data) with a fixed-budget protocol (keeping all real and past data but sampling a fixed-size subset each generation). Experiments on a 2D spiral dataset and on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 show that replacement degrades datasets rapidly, while fixed-budget training causes only partial degradation, sparing some features. It has direct implications for practitioners building iterative synthetic-data training loops, where a fixed training budget is common. The authors propose a linear-response model of multi-generational parameter dynamics analyzed via stochastic recursion, showing that some features are fragile and lost within a few generations under both protocols, while others are robust and preserved over practically unbounded horizons under the fixed-budget protocol. The study covers a 2D spiral dataset plus MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 image benchmarks.

Across eight executable agent-security benchmarks and three target-model families, PACE achieved the strictly lowest attack success rate in 62 of 79 eligible attack columns and tied in 14, while losing at most three points of native utility. Tool-using LLM agents convert generated text into real-world side effects, so poisoned tool metadata, retrieved pages, memory, or reusable skills can hijack the next call; PACE addresses this gap by enforcing security at the last boundary a deployment can still control. PACE distinguishes a certified execution contract from an evaluated configuration that can restore an authorized call after a proposed block or apply a declared repair, and confinement requires the final action to preserve the certified cut. An ablation over 1167 paired cases attributes most security gains to effect verification, while a reduced-scale adaptive search succeeded on 0/30 out-of-authority targets against the defense.

## [Discrete Wasserstein Flows Enable One-Step Generative Modeling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01355) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01355) introduces a framework for one-step generative modeling on finite state spaces by extending drifting methods beyond continuous domains using discrete Wasserstein geometry. It defines a target-relative KL gradient flow over the transitions of a reversible Markov kernel, realizes the probability flow at the particle level via Markov jumps, and amortizes the transport updates into a latent-conditioned generator so that inference requires only a single step. One-step generation is highly desirable because diffusion and flow-based models typically require many iterative sampling steps, which is computationally expensive. This work offers a principled theoretical foundation for bringing one-step generation to structured discrete data such as graphs, molecules, and text, potentially broadening the applicability of optimal-transport-based generative methods. The framework is validated in a controlled setting where the underlying distributions and transport dynamics can be computed exactly, confirming KL dissipation, consistency between particle dynamics and the probability flow, and the predicted numerical scaling. The authors also show that a finite-capacity neural generator can track these exact transport targets while retaining one-step generation, though the validation remains limited to controlled settings rather than large-scale real-world data.

One-step generative modeling aims to train a neural network that maps a simple reference distribution to the target data distribution in a single forward pass, avoiding the slow iterative sampling of diffusion and flow-matching models.

A new arXiv survey (2610.01413) systematically reviews how optimal transport (OT) is integrated into reinforcement learning objectives and algorithms, categorizing each method by the role OT plays, the distributions compared, the OT formulation used, and how temporal structure is handled. It also discusses motivations for different OT choices, practical issues like cost design and computation, and open problems such as scalable trajectory-level transport and principled mass-mismatch handling. Standard divergences like KL can become ineffective when distributions overlap weakly, a common situation in imitation learning, offline RL, and deployment under distribution shift; OT offers a geometry-aware alternative by measuring the cost of moving probability mass. This survey gives researchers in imitation learning, offline RL, and distribution-shift settings a unified map of the field and highlights where theoretical and computational gaps remain. The survey organizes methods along four axes—role of OT, distributions compared (e.g., state visitation, action, or transition distributions), OT formulation, and temporal structure treatment—and explicitly flags open challenges including scalable trajectory-level transport, principled handling of mass mismatch, and theoretical analysis for OT-regularised RL. It is a survey rather than a novel algorithmic breakthrough, so its contribution is taxonomic and conceptual.

**Background**: Optimal transport is a branch of mathematics, formalized by Monge in 1781 and later developed by Kantorovich, that studies the most efficient way to move or allocate mass from one probability distribution to another under a given ground cost. Reinforcement learning trains an agent to maximize reward through interaction with an environment, typically modeled as a Markov decision process, and many RL algorithms compare probability distributions such as policy-induced state visitation distributions or learned versus dataset action distributions. The paper reports that behavioral axes capture independent failure modes, meaning a model can be stable on one dimension while unstable on another, and that aggregate metrics can give a misleading sense of stable and reliable generalization.

A new arXiv paper (2610.01535) shows that a major LLM safety routing benchmark selects its best single-model comparator using the evaluation data itself, a bias that is harmless in-distribution but grows substantially under distribution shift. On HELM Safety the selection cost reaches 0.045-0.113 of harm under held-out categories, comparable to the entire routing deficit, and rises seven- to ninefold on AgentDojo when suites are held out. If the comparator is chosen on test labels, reported routing gains can be largely illusory, meaning safety routers may be deployed on benchmarks that overstate their real-world benefit. They also show that a model's expressed recognition of a late injection is steerable: an attacker who knows which model it faces lowers GPT-5.4's judged recognition by 19.6 points on held-out reruns.

## [Adaptive Black-Box Attack Extracts Private Image Datastores from Multimodal RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01871) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces IMMRAG, an adaptive black-box data extraction attack that reconstructs private image datastores from image-returning Multimodal RAG systems by embedding malicious instructions inside user-supplied images and steering queries through the embedding space. In a single 2500-query run, it recovered up to 611 distinct radiology images, 566 document scans, and 416 general-purpose images, reaching up to 5.6x as many distinct datastore items as a non-adaptive baseline. It highlights an urgent need for safeguards specifically designed for multimodal data. Each query blends an attacker-held shadow image with an already recovered image, and relevance-weighted resampling steers subsequent queries toward unexplored regions of the embedding space; the attack was evaluated across three scenarios (medical assistant, document helper, general-purpose tool), multiple CLIP-family retrievers, and various generators, with success measured under local-feature correspondence.

A new arXiv paper derives a convergence bound for GRPO-style algorithms under asynchronous RL and proposes Group-Mass Capping GRPO (GMC-GRPO), which minimizes a ratio-based bias bound within a class of weighted estimators. The authors prove that, compared with TIC-GRPO, GMC-GRPO improves the threshold dependence of the fourth-order delay term from O(ε⁻⁴) to O(ε⁻²) as ε→0, and experiments on Qwen3 models show better robustness to stale rollouts. Asynchronous RL is a key efficiency lever for LLM post-training, but stale rollouts from earlier policies can destabilize training, and theoretical understanding of this effect has been limited. This work provides both a convergence analysis and a practical algorithm with guarantees, offering a foundation for more efficient and stable large-scale RL post-training pipelines. The analysis shows that for trajectory-level importance-weighted estimators, once the second moment is uniformly controlled, delay enters the bound through the bias from clipping or rescaling; under local policy overlap, the delay-dependent term decreases as G^(-2/5) after tuning the step size, where G is the group size. For fixed behavior and current policies, group-rescaling bias vanishes as G→∞, whereas trajectory-wise clipping bias can persist.

The review recommends combining existing tools through binary rubric items, separate completeness and correctness scores, case-specific importance weighting with non-compensable safety caps, temporal order-consistency checks, and chance-corrected reliability reporting. ## [Mem++ Proposes Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02002) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Mem++ introduces a non-destructive memory framework that stores every document whole with its date and author, calling no generative model at write time, and instead performs read-time selection by retrieving only documents dated up to the time a question asks about. Evaluated on the organizational benchmark OrgMemBench, it surpasses the strongest memory baseline by 8.0 to 13.1 points across two answering models, and with gpt-4.1-mini achieves the best overall score, 2.6 points above RAG. Most existing memory systems compress records at write time by distilling documents into facts, notes, or graph edges, which fixes what can be answered before any question is asked and loses the ability to track how decisions changed over time. By keeping all versions and deferring selection to read time, Mem++ addresses a real limitation in long-term organizational memory and could influence future work on agent memory systems. Mem++ calls no generative model at write time and fuses lexical and semantic rankings at read time, leaving the choice among versions to the answering model rather than overwriting older ones. It also achieves the best average LLM-judge score on LoCoMo and ranks second on LongMemEval-S, behind only its own entity-graph variant, with evaluation code available on GitHub.

Researchers introduced HumanoidToolBench, an 18-task benchmark spanning three scenarios, three execution levels, and two tool-set modes, along with ToolBook, a dataset of 3.1k demonstrations collected in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 robot. Evaluation of seven policies in simulation and three on the real robot reveals substantial gaps between selecting a suitable tool and completing the task, with GR00T N1.7 probes showing reduced selection accuracy on unseen tools and continued execution under unrelated instructions. This benchmark fills a gap in evaluating humanoid robots' ability to jointly select tools, manipulate objects, and coordinate locomotion, which is essential for robots to perform tasks beyond their inherent physical limits. It provides a standardized evaluation framework and real-robot validation that could spur further research in robotics and embodied AI. The benchmark includes 18 tasks across three scenarios, three execution levels, and two tool-set modes, with demonstrations collected both in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. The GR00T N1.7 policy probes revealed two key limitations: reduced tool selection accuracy on unseen tools and continued task execution even when given unrelated instructions.

## [TESS: A Transferable Meta-Network for LLM Data Selection via Pointwise Value Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02092) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces TESS (Transferable Example Scoring and Selection), a scalable data-selection framework that replaces per-sample weights with a selection network trained under a new Pointwise Value Matching (PVM) objective. The authors show that directly plugging such a network into existing Meta-learning for Training-data Selection (MTS) objectives causes unstable optimization and poor generalization due to weight suppression and reliance on easy-to-learn features, and that PVM resolves these issues. Data selection is a major lever for reducing the cost and carbon footprint of training large language models on massive, heterogeneous corpora, and TESS claims strong transfer from subsets to full corpora and from smaller to larger models. If it holds up, this could make meta-learned data selection practical for real LLM safety and instruction-tuning pipelines rather than just small-scale experiments. The core technical contribution is the Pointwise Value Matching objective, which the authors argue avoids the weight-suppression and easy-feature-reliance failure modes of naively inserting a selection network into MTS objectives. Experiments are conducted on LLM safety and targeted instruction tuning, demonstrating transfer across datasets, subset-to-full-corpus scaling, and smaller-to-larger model scaling.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Training large language models on all available text is often suboptimal or infeasible because data quality varies widely, so researchers study data selection methods that filter or weight examples. Meta-learning for Training-data Selection (MTS) learns data weights from a target validation objective via bi-level optimization, offering a principled alternative to heuristic scoring, but it struggles with a trade-off between fine-grained valuation and transferability to unseen data. A natural fix is to replace per-sample weights with a selection network, but this paper shows that naive integration into MTS objectives fails.

## [Where-OPD: Spatially Guided Self-Distillation for Multimodal LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02117) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Where-OPD introduces a spatially guided on-policy self-distillation method for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that uses procedurally generated synthetic scenes to provide annotation-free textual guidance. The teacher model receives spatial coordinates and object identities from these synthetic scenes to locate and integrate evidence from multiple image regions, while the student learns to reproduce this behavior from the image and question alone. This work addresses a gap in applying on-policy self-distillation to MLLMs, offering a scalable, annotation-free post-training approach that avoids reliance on human-annotated grounding data or external teacher models. The demonstrated synthetic-to-real transfer suggests that spatially grounded privileged information can induce broader perceptual capabilities, potentially benefiting researchers in multimodal learning and self-distillation. The method consistently improves performance on counting, document, and chart understanding benchmarks across multiple models, and although post-training uses only synthetic scenes, it yields a 3.23-point average gain on real-world perception benchmarks including CVBench, V*, ZoomBench, BLINK, HR-Bench, and MME-RealWorld. The project page is available at https://github.com/sirkosophia/Where-OPD.

**Background**: On-policy self-distillation is a training strategy where a model self-aligns its outputs through on-policy rollouts using a self-referential teacher, such as a frozen or EMA version of itself, to mitigate exposure bias. ## [Local Support Learning: GMM-Gated Adapters Prevent Catastrophic Forgetting Without Prior Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02126) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.02126) introduces Local Support Learning (LSL), a framework that augments gradient-based training with a weight adapter plus a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) gating function that activates the adapter only on activations from the current training distribution. The authors demonstrate that this post-training approach resolves forgetting in LLMs up to 7 billion parameters, retaining both pretrained and finetuned capabilities across multiple training phases without access to prior data. Catastrophic forgetting is a central obstacle to continual learning, and most existing mitigations require storing or replaying prior data, which is often impossible due to privacy, storage, or availability constraints. LSL's ability to retain prior capabilities without any prior data, while being memory- and compute-efficient and robust to hyperparameters, could make continual fine-tuning of large pre-trained models far more practical in real-world deployments. The core challenge is that the gate must route data from all learning phases while being trained only on the current phase's data; LSL addresses this with a GMM whose likelihood decays rapidly away from its training data, giving it a natural tendency to stay closed on prior-phase inputs. The paper reports efficiency in memory and compute, robustness to hyperparameter choice, and scaling potential, though the abstract is truncated and no community discussion is available yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Catastrophic forgetting is the tendency of artificial neural networks to abruptly lose previously learned information when trained on new data, a well-documented problem since the 1990s. Continual learning research tries to let models acquire new tasks sequentially without forgetting old ones, but many methods rely on task identity or stored samples from previous tasks, which are often unavailable. Weight adapters such as LoRA are low-rank modules added to a frozen base model to enable efficient fine-tuning, and LSL builds on this idea by gating an adapter so its updates remain local to the current data distribution.

## [MIRTO: A Registration-Gated, Multiverse-Tested Evaluation Protocol for Brain MRI Anomaly Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02136) ⭐️ 7.0/10

MIRTO introduces an evaluation protocol for unsupervised anomaly detection (UAD) in brain MRI that makes explicit the typically unreported choices—registration alignment, threshold setting, false-positive budget, metric, aggregation, and lesion definition—and measures their impact. Applied to four UAD methods on 312 BraTS 2020 subjects across 15,552 evaluation pipelines, it revealed that an axis-order mismatch between stored maps and the reference dropped a diffusion model's voxel AUROC from 0.873 to 0.583 while barely affecting slice-level AUROC. This work exposes how unreported evaluation choices can drastically alter method rankings, undermining reproducibility and fair comparison in medical imaging AI. By providing a rigorous, registration-gated, multiverse-tested protocol, MIRTO could influence future benchmarking practices and lead to more reliable clinical translation of UAD methods. MIRTO gates every comparison with a registration check, sets thresholds on validation data alone, reports realized false-positive volume on test, repeats comparisons over 15,552 defensible pipelines, and attaches paired subject-bootstrap intervals with multiplicity control. Within each metric, the method explained at least 0.95 of the variance in voxel AUROC and AUPRC and 0.77 in Dice, but only 0.14 in lesion sensitivity, where lesion definition and hit criterion dominated; a training-free change to REFLECT's latent aggregation raised Dice at equal burden by 0.052.

A new arXiv paper (2610.02140) proposes a Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling algorithm that progressively transforms off-policy traces into more on-policy data given a reference model, rather than modifying the learning objective. Across scientific skill acquisition, mathematical reasoning, and open-ended expertise tasks, this sampling approach lets supervised finetuning (SFT) rival prevailing post-training techniques, often generalizing better and forgetting less than strong on-policy baselines. This challenges the conventional wisdom that reinforcement learning (RL) is necessary for strong generalization while SFT inevitably causes catastrophic forgetting, potentially offering a cheaper and more data-efficient path to post-training frontier models. If validated, it could shift how practitioners combine off-policy expert data with on-policy learning signals across the post-training stack. The method tailors the data distribution to suit the learner instead of altering the learning objective, and the resulting finetuned models show strong distributional performance, learning beyond merely sharpening the base model's distribution. The authors frame sampling as a model-native operator that shapes data for learnability, positioning it as a general-purpose primitive for the post-training stack.

A new arXiv paper (2610.02150) proposes SourceLearn, a method that lets LLM agents develop persistent, reusable understanding of a specific authoritative source instead of treating repeated use as mere repeated access. SourceLearn combines Self-Directed Source Learning, which identifies what remains incompletely understood and adaptively revisits the source, with Task-Guided Source Learning, which uses downstream task experience to expose local representational gaps and recurring organizational needs. The work reframes how agent memory and retrieval should relate to persistent knowledge sources, shifting from stateless access to accumulating source-specific competence. If it generalizes, it could improve knowledge-intensive agent workflows such as enterprise document assistants, research copilots, and domain-specific RAG systems that repeatedly query the same authoritative corpus. Across five benchmarks and three LLM backends, SourceLearn achieves the best performance in 13 of 15 settings, with gains of up to 22.6 points over Hybrid RAG and substantial improvements over static source representations and experience-based memory baselines. The orchestrator at each robot reasons over the task instruction, local observations, and messages from peers, then emits both low-level instructions for its action model and semantic messages for other robots, exploiting the complementary strengths of VLM reasoning and VLA action generation. ## [Watch, Infer, Coordinate: Inferring Robot Partner Constraints for Zero-Shot Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02170) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces "Watch, Infer, Coordinate," a benchmark and inference method that lets a helper robot infer a partner robot's physical constraints by observing it coordinate with another robot, then use that inferred capability to coordinate with the same partner on a new task. Across three physically coupled manipulation settings, the method substantially improves constraint inference and zero-shot coordination, approaching an oracle that has access to the true constraints. As robots increasingly work alongside other robots on manipulation tasks—such as carrying objects too large or heavy for one robot—a partner's hidden physical limitations from hardware degradation or actuator faults can silently break coordination. Enabling a helper to infer these constraints from joint behavior could make multi-robot teams more robust and adaptable without explicit communication or prior joint training. The core difficulty is that a demonstration shows what the constrained robot did, not what it could have done, and in physically coupled tasks the other robot may compensate for its partner's limitations, masking them from the constrained robot's behavior alone. The key insight is that constraints shape the joint behavior of the team, so both robots' actions are informative; the inference approach scores candidate constraints using observed joint behavior.

## [DMAD Recasts Distribution Matching Distillation as Adversarial Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02188) ⭐️ 7.0/10

DMAD (Distribution Matching as Adversarial Distillation) replaces DMD's auxiliary score-fitting diffusion model with two discriminator heads on a shared backbone that directly learn log-density ratios, trained via linear losses on their logits. It achieves FID 1.04 with one-step ImageNet-64x64 generation, 14.47 with four-step SDXL on COCO-10K, and a VBench score of 85.15 with four-step Wan2.1-T2V-14B, plus 79.1% and 84.6% human preference wins over DMD2 and rCM on MiniMax-H3-33B audio-video generation. This removes the memory and compute overhead of maintaining an auxiliary diffusion model in distribution-matching distillation, making few-step visual generation cheaper to train while matching or beating both few-step methods and multi-step teachers. It could accelerate adoption of fast samplers for image and video generation, where inference latency is a key bottleneck. The authors prove that at the discriminator optimum, the linear losses recover the distribution-matching gradient underlying DMD via the classical identity linking discriminator logits to log-density ratios, and they add gap-based reweighting that adapts teacher supervision across noise levels using the real-data head's empirical logit gap. Results are reported as a preprint without peer review, and the code, models, and demos are released at the project page.

**Background**: Diffusion models generate images by iteratively denoising over many steps, which is slow at inference. Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) compresses a multi-step teacher into a few-step student by matching their output distributions, but it needs an auxiliary diffusion model to estimate the student's evolving score, adding memory and compute cost. Adversarial Diffusion Distillation (ADD) instead uses a discriminator to train few-step students, and DMAD combines these ideas by treating distribution matching as a classification problem whose discriminator logits directly yield the needed log-density ratios.

A new arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.02193) introduces Hierarchical Continuous Diffusion Language Models (HC-DLM), which couple discrete token generation with a continuous latent trajectory inside a single denoising process whose training objective is derived from a variational bound on token likelihood. Discrete diffusion language models can decode tokens in parallel but sample each token independently from its marginal, severing the statistical dependencies among simultaneously decoded tokens; HC-DLM directly targets this structural bottleneck. If the reported gains hold up, the approach could make non-autoregressive diffusion language models more competitive with autoregressive generation for tasks requiring bidirectional reasoning and global constraint satisfaction. The authors evaluate HC-DLM at matched model size against both discrete and continuous diffusion baselines, reporting improvements in puzzle accuracy on Sudoku and Countdown and in generative perplexity on LM1B. The work is an arXiv preprint with a project page at https://hc-dlm.github.io/, and it has not yet undergone peer review or community validation.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Autoregressive language models generate text strictly left to right, which makes bidirectional reasoning and global constraint satisfaction awkward. Diffusion language models instead corrupt a sequence (for example by masking tokens) and learn to reverse that corruption, allowing parallel decoding; discrete variants operate directly on tokens, while continuous variants denoise a shared continuous state but only tie it to valid tokens at the final decode step. HC-DLM sits between these two families by keeping a continuous latent as the persistent generative state while continuously reading out and feeding back discrete tokens.

## [RPG Framework Lets Embodied Agents Self-Improve Without Weight Updates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02204) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers present Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real (RPG), a framework that autonomously improves robot execution systems without updating model weights by reconstructing manipulation capabilities from offline data, practicing in simulation with failure diagnosis, and transferring to real-world execution. On 22 held-out manipulation tasks, RPG raised success from 28.6% after the first practice round to 95.0% after 15 rounds, beating ASPIRE (75.5%) and CaP-Agent0 powered by GPT-6 Astra Pro (60.0%), and succeeded in all 30 physical trials after calibration. This suggests embodied agents can improve their skills through self-directed practice and symbolic skill libraries rather than expensive weight retraining, which could lower the human effort needed to build and maintain reliable robot capabilities. If the sim-to-real results hold up, it points toward more scalable, autonomous robot learning pipelines for diverse manipulation tasks. RPG uses execution feedback, privileged simulator state, and available dataset videos to diagnose failures, then develops new reusable symbolic skills, refines existing ones, and revises the system prompt; cross-task evaluation tests individual and merged revisions before retention. At test time a multimodal LLM uses the resulting system prompt and skill library to coordinate perception and robot control, and the frozen system succeeded in all 30 physical trials (ten each on three tasks) after a common calibration and hardware-adaptation procedure.

GenGait introduces a Transformer-based masked autoencoder trained exclusively on normative gait sequences from 150 adults captured via markerless multi-camera motion capture. At inference, a two-pass procedure first estimates joint inconsistency scores by occluding individual joints, then withholds flagged joints from the encoder input and reconstructs the full skeleton to produce corrected kinematic trajectories. A new arXiv paper (2604.21549v2) proves that multicalibration—calibration conditional on input features rather than just on average—is sufficient for unbiased prevalence estimation when the feature distribution shifts between populations. Simulations show standard calibration and quantification methods develop bias that grows with shift magnitude, while a multicalibrated estimator maintains near-zero bias, and two empirical applications (U.S. state employment prevalence from the American Community Survey and LLM-based political text classification across four countries) confirm substantial bias reduction. Prevalence estimation with imperfect measurement devices—diagnostic tests, classifiers, or LLMs—is fundamental to public health, science, and online trust and safety, yet standard corrections assume stable device error rates across populations. This work connects recent fairness theory to a longstanding measurement problem across disciplines, offering a theoretically grounded fix that could change how practitioners correct for bias in deployment. The theoretical guarantee applies to any classification model, not just LLMs, and the paper emphasizes that calibration data must cover the key feature dimensions along which target populations may differ. The simulation demonstrates that standard methods' bias grows with shift magnitude while the multicalibrated estimator stays near zero, though the approach's practical effectiveness depends on having representative calibration data.

## [SkillLens Organizes LLM Agent Skills into a Four-Layer Graph for Cheaper Reuse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08386) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SkillLens is a hierarchical skill-evolution framework that organizes an agent's procedural knowledge into a four-layer graph of policies, strategies, procedures, and primitives, then retrieves skills at mixed granularity. Given a task, it retrieves semantically relevant skill seeds, expands them via a degree-corrected random walk over the skill graph, and uses a verifier to accept, decompose, rewrite, or skip each visited unit, achieving up to a 6.31 percentage-point Acc@1 gain on bug localization and lifting agent success rate from 45.00% to 51.31% on MuLocbench and ALFWorld. Skill libraries are becoming the standard way for LLM agents to reuse procedural experience, but flat, single-resolution skill blocks force a trade-off between injecting irrelevant context and paying to rewrite whole skills. By reusing compatible subskills directly and adapting only locally mismatched parts, SkillLens points toward cheaper, more scalable agent memory that could lower inference costs for long-horizon agent systems. The framework provides theoretical analysis showing that mixed-granularity adaptation incurs sublinear cost under sparse mismatch assumptions, and that its evolutionary update rule monotonically improves the validation objective until a local optimum. Its verifier-driven routing is the core mechanism that decides per-unit whether to accept, decompose, rewrite, or skip, and the system also refines both multi-granularity skills and the verifier over time to improve routing decisions.

## [Consequence-Aware Compute Allocation Prioritizes High-Stakes LLM Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04402) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2606.04402v2) proposes a consequence-aware scheduler for test-time compute allocation in large language models, prioritizing tasks by the cost of failure rather than just difficulty or uncertainty. Experiments on SWE-bench Lite show that consequence-aware routing achieves the best high-consequence task success under a fixed compute budget while keeping overall accuracy competitive. Existing test-time compute strategies implicitly treat all prediction errors as equally costly, which is misaligned with real deployments where some failures cause far more damage than others. This work offers a practical way to spend limited inference compute where it matters most, benefiting production systems that must balance cost and reliability. The scheduler predicts task consequence from pre-solution inputs and routes premium compute to top-ranked tasks, since marginal gain is hard to predict before execution. A controlled within-model experiment confirms the advantage holds even when only inference attempts are reallocated, though the approach is an incremental improvement rather than a breakthrough.

**Background**: Test-time compute refers to spending extra inference-time resources—such as generating multiple samples or running iterative refinement—to improve a model's answers. Prior allocation methods decide how much compute to give each task based on difficulty, uncertainty, or expected performance gain, treating every error as equally costly. SWE-bench Lite is a benchmark of real-world software engineering tasks used to evaluate such methods.

## [Architect-Ant: Editable Automatic Furnishing of Floor Plans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10953) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces AntPlan, a curated dataset of 505 real professional architectural floor plans with dense furniture annotations spanning 92 object classes and ten residential room categories, alongside Architect-Ant, a framework that learns furnishing patterns via supervised fine-tuning and is then optimized with GRPO using a Layout Rule Score (LRS). Architect-Ant represents layouts with an editable coordinate-based DSL and generates constraint-aware furniture layouts directly, without relying on costly iterative agentic inference. Automatic furnishing has been limited by scarce real-world data and the difficulty of satisfying interacting geometric and functional constraints, so a dataset and framework that learn directly from professional plans could benefit real-estate visualization, interior design, and architectural workflows. The resulting layouts remain object-level editable and can be converted into 3D scenes, which may make AI-generated furnishing more practical for downstream design tools. The Layout Rule Score aggregates geometric and functional constraints derived from professional plans, providing outcome-level supervision without prescribed reasoning traces. Experiments against diverse state-of-the-art baselines show Architect-Ant combines low geometric violation rates with high functional completeness, and qualitative results more closely reflect real-world residential furnishing patterns.

## [SKIN-DEEP: A Geometric Diagnostic for LLM Alignment Fragility](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22676) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces SKIN-DEEP, a geometric diagnostic that examines the residual-stream activations of unmodified models, compares aligned and base checkpoints to identify safety-separating directions, and summarizes the layer-wise pattern in a Geometric Fragility Score (GFS). Validated across twenty-one instruction-tuned models, the method predicts harmful compliance after benign low-rank fine-tuning, with the lowest-scoring safe model showing the lowest harmful-compliance rate when trained on the largest tested set of harmless examples. Behavioral refusal tests only reveal alignment fragility after an intervention has already weakened safety, so a pre-fine-tuning diagnostic offers a proactive complement to refusal benchmarks. This matters for model deployment and safety evaluation, since developers could screen checkpoints for fragility before releasing them for downstream fine-tuning. Across the twenty-one instruction-tuned models, harmful requests and benign instructions exhibit a recurring low-rank separation pattern, and ablating the selected directions weakens refusal, though the effective direction varies from model to model. The code is available at https://github.com/js-lee-AI/skin-deep, and the diagnostic operates on unmodified activations without requiring any fine-tuning intervention.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: The residual stream is the running hidden-state representation that each transformer layer reads from and writes to, so its activations encode much of the model's internal state. Prior work has found that linear directions in hidden-state space can separate factual from hallucinated outputs or evaluation prompts from deployment prompts, suggesting that high-level behaviors like refusal may correspond to geometric structure. Benign fine-tuning is known to weaken safety alignment, and related work explains this fragility via a low-rank safety Fisher geometry, but SKIN-DEEP instead measures the geometry before any fine-tuning occurs.
