## [MINCE Shrinks LLM Evaluation Datasets via Monte Carlo Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22826) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces MINCE (Monte Carlo Informed N-sizing for Compact Evaluation), which uses Monte Carlo simulation over per-item logs from a small set of calibration models to find the minimum evaluation subset size that bounds accuracy drift, then freezes a randomly sampled subset at that size. It reduces IFEVAL by 54%, MMLU by 89%, GSM8K by 70%, and MMLU-Pro by 88% with maximum drift of 2.62 percentage points on BF16 calibration models. Evaluating many LLM variants—quantized, fine-tuned, or deployment-specific—currently requires rerunning large benchmarks that can take tens of hours per model on edge hardware such as NPUs. MINCE cuts this cost dramatically while keeping accuracy estimates reliable, which could make frequent, deployment-specific evaluation practical for researchers and practitioners. The frozen subsets generalize to held-out GPU models with mean drift ≤1.40 pp and to INT4 NPU models with mean drift of 0.77–3.59 pp, delivering up to 8.1× speedup on GPU models and 1.7–3.4× on NPU models. MINCE achieves lower drift than tinyBenchmarks (12× lower on MMLU, 3.3× on GSM8K) while using 42× fewer calibration models, and it requires no learned prediction layer.

**Background**: Monte Carlo methods are a broad class of computational algorithms that use repeated random sampling to obtain numerical results, often applied to problems too complex for exact mathematical analysis. LLM evaluation benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, IFEVAL, and MMLU-Pro are standardized tests that measure model capabilities like knowledge, math reasoning, and instruction following, but running them fully is expensive. ## [New Law Predicts LLM Ensemble Lift from Diversity of Thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.17384) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper derives an exact decomposition of LLM ensemble lift into "rescue" and "damage" masses, yielding a compact heuristic based on an accuracy-adjusted correctness correlation (phi_adj), accuracy gap, and collective accuracy. The law was validated on 767,520 inferences from ten open-weight models across SuperGPQA, GPQA Diamond, and a novel agentic cybersecurity benchmark, with the heuristic calibrated on SuperGPQA at a 40:60 vote split achieving Spearman's rho = 0.84 and transferring to unseen datasets (rho = 0.51 on GPQA Diamond, 0.84 on forensic tasks). This work gives researchers and practitioners a quantitative, pre-pooling predictor for when combining multiple LLMs will actually help, potentially saving compute and guiding ensemble design. It also introduces a novel agentic cybersecurity benchmark with 23,520 graded trials and releases all votes openly, supporting reproducibility and further study of diversity of thought in LLMs. Raw correctness correlation phi has almost no predictive power (R^2 <= 0.09), while the accuracy-adjusted phi_adj is markedly superior (R^2 = 0.67 on SuperGPQA), and the measured swap mass tracks realized lift with R^2 >= 0.96 throughout. The heuristic's coefficients are frozen after calibration on SuperGPQA, and it remains the most stable pre-pooling predictor across all three datasets.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: LLM ensembles combine outputs from multiple models, often by majority voting, to improve reasoning accuracy over any single model. The benefit depends on "diversity of thought"—models making different errors so that correct answers can be rescued—but until now there was no formal law predicting how much uplift a given pair or group of models would provide. SuperGPQA is a large graduate-level benchmark spanning 285 disciplines, and GPQA Diamond is a challenging subset of graduate-level science questions; both are used here to test the predictive law.

## [Semantic Cooperative Games: Fast Contribution Attribution for LLM Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.18255) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2607.18255v2) proposes Semantic Cooperative Games (SCG), a framework that represents a realized language flow as a semantic generation hypergraph and defines a Semantic Shapley Value (SSV) to attribute agent contributions. It introduces SLIC, a single-trajectory algorithm that builds the hypergraph, recovers minimal semantic supports, applies Boolean absorption, and computes SSV without rerunning agent subsets, cutting computation cost by 93.3% on a medical benchmark while staying highly consistent with a Monte Carlo Shapley baseline. Contribution attribution is a central problem in LLM-based multi-agent systems, where outputs emerge from many agents, message exchanges, and ordered workflow dependencies, and existing counterfactual methods require repeated model calls and introduce high variance. A fast, counterfactual-free, and interpretable attribution method could improve debugging, credit assignment, and failure analysis in complex multi-agent pipelines, benefiting researchers in multi-agent systems and explainable AI. The authors prove that SSV reduces to the classical Shapley value under standard set-based, fully observable, and no-order-dependence conditions, and on a medical benchmark satisfying these conditions SLIC achieves the 93.3% cost reduction. In more general multi-role workflows, SSV aligns with perturbation-induced score-drop profiles and reveals cases where semantic contribution and failure impact diverge, though the work remains a preprint without community discussion yet.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: The Shapley value is a cooperative game theory solution concept that fairly distributes total gains or costs among players according to their marginal contribution across all possible coalitions, and it is widely used in economics, finance, and machine learning for attribution. A hypergraph generalizes a graph by allowing edges to connect any number of nodes, and semantic hypergraphs use this structure to represent natural-language meaning and hierarchical relations. LLM-based multi-agent systems typically involve specialized agents interacting through structured workflows, often modeled as directed acyclic graphs, which makes attributing credit or blame to individual agents difficult.

Researchers released ESCROW, a post-deployment maintenance framework that updates an LLM agent's external, reviewable skills under a Strict Update Boundary, where the LLM only proposes candidate revisions and solely an empirically evaluated version is deployed. In real production on an internal financial document-auditing system, ESCROW achieved the strongest evaluated accuracy-cost trade-off among baselines, with a transfer probe on the public τ-bench. Enterprise LLM agents run policy-bound workflows where a careless update can sacrifice one task category's accuracy, revive a resolved failure, or land at an undeployable cost, so ESCROW's guarded, auditable update process directly addresses a major blocker to long-term agent deployment. It matters to teams operating agents in regulated domains such as finance, where consistency and auditability are mandatory. ESCROW combines distributed diagnosis with consensus, a per-category non-regression guard, cross-cycle anti-regression, and accuracy-cost Pareto search, emitting a versioned, auditable diff for each change. The paper is an arXiv preprint (2608.01772v2) with no community discussion yet, and its production evidence comes from a single internal financial document-auditing system plus a transfer probe on τ-bench.

## [Full-Bandwidth Transformer Adds Latent Feedback Between Decoding Steps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08888) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper introduces the 'full-bandwidth transformer,' which at each autoregressive decoding step fuses the previous top-layer hidden state with the sampled token embedding via a gated linear unit and feeds the result back as the next input. The authors train 1B-parameter models on up to 400B tokens using a scheduled multi-pass objective that introduces latent feedback late in pretraining, and report improvements in validation loss, 5-shot evaluation, math and coding generation, and instruction-tuned performance. The work targets a real architectural limitation — the narrow vertical feedback channel in autoregressive transformers — while preserving standard components, the KV cache, and the language-modeling objective, making it easy to adopt. If the reported gains hold, latent feedback could influence future LLM architecture research by letting non-verbalized computation re-enter the stack with a renewed depth budget. Latent feedback is trained without losing parallel teacher forcing by introducing it late in pretraining and mixing a small fraction of deeper feedback passes for stability. With negligible per-token decoding overhead, the models match or approach standard transformers trained with roughly 1.5x more tokens, and produce shorter reasoning when no off-policy templates are provided.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Autoregressive transformers compute along two axes: horizontally across generated tokens and vertically through model depth. Dense attention gives each token broad horizontal access to the past, but the vertical feedback channel between decoding steps is narrow — only the sampled token returns to the bottom of the stack while the top-layer hidden state is discarded. A gated linear unit (GLU) is a neural network component that gates one linear projection with another, and the KV cache stores key-value vectors so autoregressive models avoid recomputing attention over previous tokens. Teacher forcing is the standard training technique of feeding ground-truth tokens as inputs rather than the model's own predictions.

## [Paper Proposes Risk-Informed World Models for Safety-Critical Embodied AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03774) ⭐️ 7.0/10

An arXiv perspective paper (2609.03774v2) argues that current world models optimize for predictive likelihood and visual fidelity rather than safety-relevant evidence, and proposes the Risk-Informed World Model (RIWM) as a decision-centric alternative. RIWM organizes world modeling around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability, integrating decision-relevant representation, counterfactual reasoning, safety-critical episodic memory, and runtime safety assurance. The paper identifies three structural mismatches in current world modeling—likelihood versus risk, prediction versus intervention, and finite-horizon prediction versus accumulated consequences—that could mislead safety-critical embodied systems such as robots and autonomous vehicles. By reframing world models around which futures matter rather than which are likely, it could shape future research agendas in AI safety and embodied AI. RIWM distinguishes physical, social, and operational consequences while using epistemic uncertainty to qualify the evidence supporting action, and it raises open challenges in identifying consequential futures, validating counterfactual reasoning, maintaining revisable safety memories, translating learned consequences into executable constraints, and determining when evidence is sufficient to act. As a perspective piece, it offers a conceptual research direction rather than empirical results or a deployed system.

**Background**: World models are internal representations that let an AI system simulate and predict how an environment will evolve, and recent work has advanced them from compact latent dynamics to generative, controllable, interactive simulators. In safety-critical embodied settings, a model that maximizes predictive likelihood may overlook rare but high-risk events, because high likelihood and visual fidelity do not guarantee that safety-relevant evidence is preserved. Counterfactual reasoning—reasoning about hypothetical scenarios and the consequences of alternative actions—is widely regarded as important for AI safety, and RIWM builds on this idea by making consequences and intervention central to world modeling.

## [SE-GoS: Self-Evolving Graph-of-Skills for LLM Agent Skill Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.08228) ⭐️ 7.0/10

SE-GoS introduces a self-evolving graph-of-skills that treats the retrieval graph as an index maintained from execution traces, rather than a learned representation. On SkillsBench, one evolution round raises average reward from 52.4% to 59.4%, outperforming full-library loading, vector retrieval, static GoS, and SkillDAG across three backbones, while using about two-thirds of the input tokens of full-library loading. As LLM agent skill libraries grow to thousands of entries, retrieval becomes the bottleneck, and SE-GoS shows the retrieval graph can be improved purely from execution experience without model training, retrieval-algorithm changes, or skill-content edits. This offers a practical, low-cost path to scaling agent skill libraries and could immediately benefit agent frameworks that rely on large reusable skill sets. SE-GoS applies three updates: topology (inducing relations from execution evidence and retracting an avoid edge only after repeated successful co-use), edge-weight (softly attenuating unsupported semantic edges and reinforcing incoming edges to used skills), and node-description (updating retrieval-facing descriptions on low-ranked nodes). The evolved graph improves a held-out split it never saw from 52.9% to 58.3%, showing transfer rather than memorization, though repeating the evolution round does not help further.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: LLM agents increasingly rely on large libraries of reusable skills, but at thousands of entries, deciding which skills to load becomes the bottleneck. Graph-of-Skills (GoS) retrieves dependency-aware bundles from a typed skill graph, and SkillDAG showed such a graph can accumulate execution-backed structure online. SE-GoS asks whether execution traces can be distilled into a better retrieval graph that generalizes to unseen tasks, treating the graph as an index while keeping the retrieval pipeline, skill library, and model fixed.

## [Kernel-Managed Shared Memory Boosts Multi-Agent Personalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.10144) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.10144v2) introduces kernel-managed shared memory, a system-level abstraction in which specialized agents write structured, tagged memories while the agent-system kernel—not individual agents—governs retrieval, privacy enforcement, and prompt injection. Implemented on AIOS and tested across GPT-4o, Llama-3.1:8B, and Qwen-2.5:7B in 1,800 trials, it improved personalization scores by 2.4–4.0 points on a 5-point scale versus an unmanaged Mem0 backend, with all comparisons significant at p < 10^-18. The results suggest that centralizing memory management in the agent-system kernel, rather than leaving retrieval and privacy enforcement to individual agents, delivers most of the personalization benefit of unconstrained context at a fraction of the cost. This could shape how multi-agent AI frameworks handle shared context, privacy, and prompt-injection risk as agent deployments scale. Against full, unfiltered context concatenation, kernel-managed injection statistically matched performance on two of three models and showed a small, model-specific deficit on the third, while cutting end-to-end latency by 15–61% and reducing per-call token usage and inference cost. The evaluation used identical underlying storage for the kernel-managed and Mem0 conditions, isolating the effect of kernel governance rather than storage quality.

## [FOCUS trains LLMs to revise intermediate solutions for structured reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33149) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2609.33149v2) introduces FOCUS (Frontier-Oriented Curation Using Self-trajectories), a training method that selects intermediate candidate solution states from a model's own reasoning trajectories where it can make substantial progress within a fixed number of recurrent updates. Coupling a pretrained LLM backbone with a recurrent updater, the approach achieves 64.4% exact solve accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme and 91.1% on Maze-Hard with Qwen3-1.7B, with similar gains across five Qwen and Llama backbones from 1.7B to 8B parameters. This work connects the educational principle of "desirable difficulty" to LLM training, showing that curating training states at the model's current frontier of achievable progress can substantially improve constraint-satisfaction reasoning. It also reports zero-shot transfer to mathematical reasoning and code execution even when the recurrent updater is disabled, suggesting the approach may generalize beyond the puzzle domains it was trained on. The recurrent updater reuses the same parameters at every update step, and FOCUS measures how much the model improves each state within a fixed number of recurrent updates, prioritizing states with substantial progress. The paper is an arXiv preprint without peer review, and the reported results are limited to Sudoku, maze solving, and the tested Qwen/Llama backbones.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku and maze solving are constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs), where a set of variables must be assigned values satisfying a collection of constraints. Unlike free-form chain-of-thought, these tasks allow a model to iteratively revise an explicit candidate solution until it satisfies all constraints, making intermediate states natural training examples. Recurrent neural networks process sequential data by feeding outputs back as inputs at each step, and this paper adapts that idea into a recurrent updater that repeatedly revises a solution state.

A new arXiv preprint (2609.34024v2) evaluates Jev 1.13, TypeSafe AI's non-generative "System One" model that assigns probabilities to predefined answer options, across four medical benchmarks: MetaMedQA, PubMedQA, DiagnosisArena-MCQ, and the NEJM Case Challenges. Jev matched GPT-6 Sol with medium reasoning on PubMedQA (78.4% vs 78.2%) but trailed on MetaMedQA (74.8% vs 82.7%) and fell far behind on DiagnosisArena-MCQ (59.8% vs 82.4%) and NEJM cases (61.8% vs 82.4%). This underscores that task-specific validation, not general benchmark scores, must precede any clinical deployment of such models. Jev was best calibrated on MetaMedQA (expected calibration error 0.063 vs 0.146 for GPT-6 Sol), and its answers with probability ≥0.9 (52.9% of questions) were 93.4% accurate, though GPT-6 Sol matched this when accepting a similar share of questions; on DiagnosisArena-MCQ its probability discrimination was poor (AUROC 0.645 vs 0.768). All 8,469 requests returned valid answers, median latency was 0.27–0.31 s, and all 2,823 items cost just USD 0.08, but Jev recognized only 10.5% of the 162 unanswerable questions versus 8.6% for GPT-6 Sol.

Researchers introduce Stratified Inoculation Prompting (SIP), a fine-tuning technique that uses a small clean subset of training examples and oversamples them under diverse non-eliciting prompts while inoculating the rest. SIP substantially reduces undesired behavior expression while preserving more desired behavior than standard Inoculation Prompting (IP), and yields lower emergent misalignment rates across all harmful-advice setups tested. This work addresses a key limitation of Inoculation Prompting—undesired behavior still leaking under unrelated prompts and desired behavior being hindered—which matters for AI safety researchers and practitioners fine-tuning language models with imperfect data. SIP's gains persist even when IP is extended to oversample the same clean subset at the same rate, and SIP can be further extended with backdoor dilution (weakening expression under the inoculation prompt) and password-locked inoculation (concentrating elicitation on a designated password). The approach specifically targets settings where both desired and undesired behaviors co-occur in most training examples, leaving only a small clean subset after filtering.

The Fréchet mean is a generalization of the arithmetic mean to arbitrary metric spaces, defined as the point minimizing the expected squared distance to a set of points.

Researchers propose Forward Target Propagation (FTP), a biologically plausible training method that replaces backpropagation's backward pass with a second forward pass, estimating layerwise targets using only feedforward computations. ## [FairSSL: Fair Multimodal Self-Supervised Learning via Subject-Aware VICReg](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16748) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers propose FairSSL, a framework that challenges the common redundancy assumption in multimodal self-supervised learning by treating data heterogeneity as a resource for fairness. It introduces a subject-aware Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization (VICReg) objective with segment-based pooling for variable-length modalities, and theoretical analysis shows the objective bounds the score gap between protected groups. This work is significant because it addresses fairness in multimodal self-supervised learning, a setting where enforcing strict alignment across views can discard modality-specific signals and amplify bias, which is especially relevant for real-world applications like healthcare and behavioral data. It offers a principled way to improve fairness without sacrificing downstream predictive performance. FairSSL uses a subject-aware VICReg objective that enforces alignment across segments from the same subject, a segment-based pooling strategy for variable-length modalities, and regularization to encourage within-subject variability, cross-modal and cross-subject invariance, and representation decorrelation. Code is available at https://github.com/abtinmU/FairSSL.

## [Continuous Objectives Drive Compositional Generalization in Visual Generative Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03075) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A systematic study (arXiv:2510.03075) isolates independent design axes in image and video generation and identifies two key factors for compositional generalization: whether the training objective operates on a discrete or continuous distribution, and the completeness of conditioning information about constituent factors during training. The authors also show that adding an auxiliary continuous latent loss can partially recover compositional performance in discrete models such as MaskGIT. Compositional generalization—generating novel combinations of known concepts—is a central open challenge for generative AI, and this work suggests that simply shifting from discrete to continuous training objectives may be a broadly applicable fix. The findings are corroborated across diverse compositional tasks in image and video generation, with preliminary evidence in world models and LLMs, making the recommendation relevant well beyond visual generation. The study isolates independent design axes to attribute compositional success to specific choices rather than confounded factors, and it demonstrates that relaxing a discrete loss with an auxiliary continuous latent objective yields partial—not full—recovery in MaskGIT. Evidence in world models and LLMs is described as preliminary, so the generality of the conclusion remains to be fully established.

**Background**: Compositional generalization refers to a model's ability to produce correct outputs for unseen combinations of concepts it has only seen separately during training, such as generating a red cube next to a blue sphere after training on red spheres and blue cubes. Visual generative models are commonly built either on continuous objectives, like diffusion models that denoise continuous latents, or on discrete objectives, like MaskGIT, which learns to predict randomly masked image tokens and refines them iteratively at inference. Researchers introduced the Behavioral Constant-Time Motion Planner (B-CTMP), which extends Constant-Time Motion Planning (CTMP) to two-step manipulation tasks where a collision-free motion is followed by a stochastic behavior such as grasping or insertion. B-CTMP was evaluated on three manipulation tasks—shelf picking, plug insertion, and wheel replacement—in simulation and on real robots, where its certified plans succeeded consistently while baselines failed during behavior execution, and it rejected infeasible object poses in constant time. For deterministic behaviors, a single rollout suffices, recovering the binary reachability check of prior CTMP as a special case.

## [InterviewSim: Scalable Interview-Grounded Personality Simulation for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.20294) ⭐️ 7.0/10

InterviewSim introduces a large-scale evaluation framework for personality simulation in LLMs, built on over 671,000 question-answer pairs extracted from 23,000 verified interview transcripts covering 1,000 public personalities, each averaging 11.5 hours of interview content. It proposes four complementary metrics—content similarity, factual consistency, personality alignment, and factual knowledge retention—and finds that interview grounding consistently improves content alignment and exact-match factual recall over biographical profiles and parametric prompting. This work addresses a key gap in personality simulation research: existing evaluations rely on demographic surveys, personality questionnaires, or short AI-led interviews rather than direct comparison against what individuals actually said. By providing a large-scale, interview-grounded benchmark and metric suite, it enables principled method selection and could become a standard reference for evaluating LLM-based persona and character simulation. The framework reveals complementary strengths among methods: retrieval-augmented approaches tend to preserve personality alignment, while larger chronological contexts generally reduce contradictions and improve factual recall. The four metrics are designed to be complementary, so no single method dominates across all dimensions, and the dataset's scale (671k QA pairs, 23k transcripts) makes it one of the largest interview-grounded resources for this task.

## [ProtoDCS: Robust Open-Set Test-Time Adaptation for VLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.23653) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2602.23653v3) introduces ProtoDCS, a prototype-based double-check separation framework for open-set test-time adaptation (OSTTA) of vision-language models. It replaces brittle hard thresholds with probabilistic Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) verification and uses an evidence-driven adaptation strategy with uncertainty-aware loss and efficient prototype-level updates, achieving state-of-the-art results on CIFAR-10/100-C and Tiny-ImageNet-C. Existing VLM-based test-time adaptation methods assume closed-set test streams, so they fail when unknown out-of-distribution samples appear alongside shifted in-distribution data. ProtoDCS addresses this practically important open-set scenario, enabling safer and more efficient deployment of VLMs under real-world distribution shifts. The method's double-check separation uses GMM verification to distinguish covariate-shifted in-distribution (csID) from covariate-shifted out-of-distribution (csOOD) samples, while the adaptation strategy mitigates overconfidence and reduces computational overhead via prototype-level updates. Code is promised at https://github.com/O-YangF/ProtoDCS, though the work is still a preprint without peer review or community discussion.

Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to adjust a pre-trained model during inference without labels, and open-set TTA (OSTTA) further requires separating unknown out-of-distribution samples from known in-distribution ones. The paper introduces Large Reward Models (LRMs), a framework that fine-tunes a state-of-the-art vision-language model on a multi-source dataset of real robot trajectories, human-object interactions, and simulated manipulation environments to produce frame-level rewards. LRMs expose three reward interfaces — progress estimation, task completion, and temporal contrastive comparison — and using progress rewards to guide PPO refinement improves an imitation-learned policy on held-out long-horizon tasks, while progress-weighted behavioral cloning beats SFT on four real-world manipulation tasks across two robot platforms. Reward specification is a core bottleneck for applying reinforcement learning to robotics, and this work shows that modality-specialized foundation VLMs can supply reusable, non-privileged visual reward signals without hand-coded task rewards. If it generalizes, it could let robots self-improve from their own visual observations in both simulation and the physical world, lowering the engineering cost of RL-based manipulation. LRM progress rewards are reported as the strongest non-privileged online refinement signal, improving the imitation-learning baseline and narrowing the gap to privileged environment rewards, though they do not fully match privileged rewards. The approach is validated on held-out long-horizon simulated tasks and four real-world tasks on two robot platforms, but the abstract does not report absolute success rates or comparisons against other VLM-based reward baselines.

## [LLMs Show Higher Volatility and Action Bias Than Humans in Group Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.02578) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2604.02578v2) compares LLM and human behavior in a common-interest game called Group Binary Search, where n players independently submit numbers to collectively hit a randomly assigned target without direct communication. The study finds that LLMs, unlike humans, fail to stabilize their behavior over time, exhibit excessive switching, and benefit little from richer feedback, though GRPO training can reduce the excessive switching. This work provides a behaviorally grounded diagnostic for understanding why LLM groups converge poorly in multi-agent coordination tasks, which is critical as LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that must cooperate. The findings suggest that current LLMs lack the adaptive stabilization strategies humans naturally use, highlighting a key limitation for multi-agent AI systems. The paper introduces mechanism-level metrics such as reactivity scaling, switching dynamics, and learning across games to quantify the differences. Richer feedback (e.g., numerical error magnitude) substantially improves human performance but has only small effects on LLMs, and GRPO—a reinforcement learning method—can effectively reduce LLM excessive switching.

## [Exact Operator Framework Links Forgetting to Task Distribution in Continual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.13460) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2604.13460v2) introduces an exact operator identity that expresses historical forgetting in continual learning directly in terms of the task distribution, rather than the order in which tasks are presented. Under i.i.d. task sampling and sequential exact fitting in overparameterized linear regression, the authors prove an exponential decay guarantee for expected forgetting and derive a lower bound on recovery time for individual tasks. This work shifts the theoretical lens from task ordering to task distribution structure, potentially offering a more fundamental explanation of catastrophic forgetting and guiding the design of task curricula or data streams that minimize forgetting. It is likely to interest researchers in continual learning, optimization, and learning theory. The framework assumes a shared solution, i.i.d. task sampling, and sequential exact fitting in finite-dimensional overparameterized linear regression; the exponential decay rate is tied to how well the task distribution covers observable directions, and the authors construct a distribution achieving inverse-coverage scaling for recovery time. As a preprint, the results are theoretical and have not yet been peer-reviewed or validated on deep neural networks.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Continual learning refers to training models on a non-stationary stream of tasks, where neural networks often suffer catastrophic forgetting—a drastic drop in performance on earlier tasks after learning new ones. Operator theory studies linear operators on function spaces and provides tools for analyzing how transformations act on high-dimensional data. Overparameterized linear regression, where the number of parameters exceeds the number of data points, is a common theoretical testbed for understanding generalization and forgetting because it admits exact analytical solutions.

## [TRACE Method Cuts Clinical Note Bloat to Boost LLM Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16364) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced TRACE, a method that uses note-level EHR metadata to strip templated and copied text from clinical notes, with frequency-based de-duplication as a fallback when metadata are unavailable. Evaluated across 5.3 million notes from liver transplant, obstetrics, and inpatient cohorts at multiple health systems, TRACE removed 47.3% of chart text (742.7 million characters) for 1,000 sampled Stanford Health Care patients while preserving information extraction and clinical prediction performance. Note bloat dilutes clinical signal and inflates LLM inference costs, so TRACE's ability to cut nearly half of chart text while maintaining task performance could substantially lower the cost of deploying clinical AI at scale. Projected three-year net savings ranged from $1.00M to $13.58M at a large tertiary academic center, making this a practical contribution to healthcare AI economics. Blinded physician span review found that only 0.3–6.6% of removed text was author-generated, and TRACE captured 86% of annotated templated characters. Information extraction F1 differences ranged from -0.009 to +0.004, and task-specific prediction F1 differences ranged from -0.011 to +0.018, indicating no meaningful degradation; TRACE also averaged 220,167 fewer tokens per patient.

## [Rewind-IL: Training-Free Online Failure Detection and State Respawning for Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16683) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Rewind-IL introduces a training-free online safeguard framework for generative action-chunked imitation policies, combining a zero-shot failure detector called Temporal Inter-chunk Discrepancy Estimate (TIDE) calibrated with split conformal prediction, and a state-respawning mechanism that rewinds the robot to a semantically verified safe intermediate state. Experiments on real-world and simulated long-horizon manipulation tasks, including transfer to flow-matching action-chunked policies, show that policy-internal consistency coupled with semantically grounded respawning improves reliability. Deployment failures remain a major obstacle for imitation learning, especially for long-horizon action-chunked policies that continue producing locally plausible actions after drifting off the demonstration manifold. Rewind-IL offers a practical, training-free route to improved reliability for robotics and ML practitioners, addressing a known failure mode without requiring failure data or retraining. The detector monitors self-consistency in overlapping action chunks and tracks similarity to a compact checkpoint feature database built offline using a vision-language model to identify recovery checkpoints and the frozen policy encoder to construct features. Upon failure, execution rewinds to the latest verified safe state before restarting inference from a clean policy state, and the approach transfers to flow-matching action-chunked policies.

**Background**: Imitation learning enables robots to acquire complex visuomotor manipulation skills from demonstrations, and action-chunked policies improve temporal consistency by predicting short sequences of future actions rather than single actions. Conformal prediction is a distribution-free uncertainty quantification technique that produces statistically valid prediction sets or intervals, while vision-language models jointly interpret images and text and are used here to identify recovery checkpoints in demonstrations.

A new arXiv paper (2604.18572v3) re-examines the Platonic Representation Hypothesis and finds that evidence for cross-modal representational convergence is substantially weaker than previously claimed. The authors show that the mutual k-nearest-neighbor metric used on 1024 text-image pairs captures only coarse structure, and that alignment saturates for recent language models. This work challenges a significant claim in multimodal AI that modality choice may not matter, and suggests that full representational convergence would require fine-grained alignment that current models do not achieve. It has implications for how researchers interpret cross-modal alignment and design future representation learning studies. The paper notes that to prevent alignment from collapsing as data scales, k must grow proportionally, undercutting fine-grained convergence; that one-to-one text-image pairing favors alignment while non-bijective data decreases it; and that neither stronger language models nor richer captions yield fine-grained alignment.

## [Compute Aligned Training Aligns LLM Training with Test-Time Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.24957) ⭐️ 7.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2604.24957v3) proposes Compute Aligned Training, a method that treats test-time inference strategies as operators on the base policy and derives new loss functions for both Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) that maximize performance when those strategies are applied. The authors report empirical evidence that this approach substantially improves test-time scaling compared with standard post-training. Standard SFT and RL optimize the likelihood of individual samples under a base policy, which is misaligned with test-time procedures that aggregate or filter multiple outputs, so this work could make post-training more directly reward the way models are actually used at inference. If the gains hold, it may influence how future LLMs are fine-tuned for reasoning and other test-time-compute-heavy tasks. The paper conceptualizes inference strategies as operators on the base policy and instantiates the derived loss functions for SFT and RL across common test-time strategies, though it is an arXiv preprint without peer review and the abstract does not specify model sizes, benchmarks, or the magnitude of the reported gains.

**Background**: Test-time scaling (TTS) refers to allocating additional computation during inference — for example by sampling many candidate answers and then aggregating or filtering them — rather than relying only on computation spent during training, and it has become a major way to boost LLM reasoning. Post-training typically uses Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), which updates a pretrained model on labeled input-output pairs with a token-level cross-entropy loss, and Reinforcement Learning (RL), which optimizes a reward signal; both generally maximize the likelihood of individual samples under a base policy. This creates a mismatch when inference instead depends on aggregated or filtered outputs, which is the gap Compute Aligned Training aims to close.

LensVLM is an inference framework and post-training recipe that lets Vision Language Models scan compressed images of text and selectively expand only relevant regions to their uncompressed form via learned tools. Built on Qwen3.5-9B-Base, it maintains accuracy comparable to the full-text upper bound at 4.3x effective compression and outperforms retrieval-based, text- and visual-compression baselines up to 10.1x effective compression across seven text QA benchmarks. This addresses a key limitation of VLM-based text processing: accuracy collapses as rendered characters shrink below the vision encoder's effective resolution. By achieving high compression while preserving accuracy, LensVLM could significantly reduce token and compute costs for long-context document understanding and multimodal processing. The approach generalizes to multimodal document and code understanding tasks, with the accuracy gain over baselines growing as compression increases. Analysis shows training makes visual compression robust to rendering choices, and as compression grows the model increasingly relies on expanded content rather than unreliable visual reading; text expansion is preferable for rendered text, while high-resolution image expansion suits native documents whose layout cues carry task-relevant information.

Researchers introduce POISE (Policy Optimization with Internal State Value Estimation), a reinforcement learning algorithm that replaces the traditional value critic with a lightweight probe reading the model's own internal states during the forward pass. GPart introduces a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that maps a d-dimensional trainable vector directly into the full weight space using a sparse, isometric partition matrix, avoiding LoRA's bilinear non-isometry. It requires only a single main hyperparameter (d) and a minimal checkpoint consisting of the trainable vector plus a random seed. This work addresses a fundamental geometric limitation of LoRA-based PEFT, potentially simplifying model selection and enabling more compact adapter composition. It could benefit researchers and practitioners fine-tuning large models under ultra-low parameter budgets across NLP, vision, and reasoning tasks. GPart matches or improves over existing PEFT methods at ultra-low parameter budgets across natural language understanding, computer vision, and mathematical reasoning benchmarks. It retains a fixed global parameter-sharing prior and removes the low-rank reconstruction used by LoRA-based methods, providing exact end-to-end isometry and a predictable geometry between trainable coordinates and weight updates.

## [Credal LLMs Use LoRA Ensembles to Quantify Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.23244) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Credal Large Language Models (CLLMs), which use an ensemble of LoRA adapters to induce a credal set whose lower and upper probabilities expose the spread of plausible predictive distributions instead of collapsing to a single softmax output. It derives a single commitment rule that commits to an answer only when its lower probability exceeds the upper probability of every alternative, otherwise returning the set of answers no plausible predictor rules out, applied as Credal Token Commitment (CTC), credal decoding, and Credal Semantic Commitment (CSC). This addresses a significant limitation of standard LLMs—overconfidence and the conflation of epistemic ignorance with genuine ambiguity—and could influence future work on reliable LLM deployment by enabling principled abstention or set-valued answers. It matters for anyone deploying LLMs in high-stakes settings where knowing when the model does not know is as important as the answer itself. Evaluated with Gemma-2-9B, Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B on OpenBookQA, CoQA, TriviaQA and ARC-Challenge, CTC commits on 73-91% of multiple-choice questions at 89-98% accuracy and returns sets of 1.1-1.5 options containing the gold one on 89-98%, with intervals containing observed accuracy in 24 of 30 confidence bins without calibration; corrupted context lowers commitment from 87-92% to 65-71%, and on open-ended QA CLLM outperforms semantic entropy and Laplace-LoRA by up to 19% and 9.5% absolute accuracy on CoQA and TriviaQA with context.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: A credal set is a set of probability distributions (often closed and convex) used to express uncertainty about which probabilistic model should be used, and it naturally combines epistemic uncertainty (lack of knowledge) with aleatoric uncertainty (statistical randomness). LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that adds small trainable low-rank matrices to a frozen pre-trained model, making it cheap to train and store many adapters. Standard LLMs represent uncertainty through a single predictive distribution, which conflates epistemic ignorance with genuine ambiguity; CLLMs instead use an ensemble of LoRA adapters to form a credal set and apply a commitment rule to decide when to answer or return a set of plausible answers.

## [ESNN: Equivariant Sheaf Neural Networks Learn Directed Matrix Transport on Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.28853) ⭐️ 7.0/10

Researchers introduced ESNN (Equivariant Sheaf Neural Network), a first-order architecture that learns directed, matrix-valued transport between neighboring vector features while preserving exact Euclidean (E(n)) equivariance. The paper theoretically proves that when relative displacement is the only covariant geometric input, every linear O(n)-equivariant transport map decomposes into independent radial and tangential components, and it introduces a controlled symmetry-relaxation mechanism for systems with a preferred ambient direction. This offers a complementary route to expressive equivariant message passing without resorting to computationally expensive higher-order representations, which could benefit molecular property prediction, particle dynamics, mesh simulation, and point-cloud classification. It also bridges two previously separate lines of work — sheaf neural networks, which use matrix-valued maps but ignore physical symmetries, and equivariant GNNs, which respect symmetries but move vectors with scalars. ESNN keeps scalar and vector features first-order and places the added geometric flexibility in the edge transport itself, and its symmetry relaxation can either prescribe or infer a preferred direction from data while recovering full E(n)-equivariance when that directional pathway is inactive. Experiments show improved dynamics prediction, recovery of the gravity axis when symmetry is broken, substantial gains on selected mesh tasks and long-horizon rollouts, and robustness to unseen rotations.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Equivariant graph neural networks are designed so that rotating or translating the input geometry rotates or translates the learned features in a corresponding way, which is important for modeling physical systems. Sheaf neural networks instead attach vector spaces to nodes and edges and use matrix-valued maps to describe how features are transported along edges, allowing asymmetric and non-constant relations. ESNN combines these two ideas by making the sheaf-like edge transport itself equivariant, and the paper's theory characterizes exactly what form such linear transport can take when only relative displacement is available as geometric input.

## [DOHF Turns Doob's h-Transform into Online Diffusion Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.31882) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces DOHF (Diffusion Online h-guidance Fine-tuning), which converts Doob's h-transform into a practical online training algorithm that assigns optimality weights to generated samples, estimates the normalized local correction ∇log h under the current rollout policy, and distills it directly into the generative model. The authors also provide a unified h-transform perspective that characterizes the population-optimal DiffusionNFT update and various classifier-free guidance methods. This work offers a theoretically grounded way to align diffusion models with black-box, non-differentiable rewards without extra network evaluations, which could make reward-based fine-tuning cheaper and more practical for tasks where desirable outcomes are rare. It also bridges probabilistic conditioning theory and reinforcement-learning-style fine-tuning, relevant to both the diffusion and RL communities. DOHF accommodates black-box and non-differentiable rewards without additional network evaluations, and the authors report improved alignment across three empirical scenarios spanning statistical sampling and visual generation. The method relies on inexpensive estimation of ∇log h and iterative distillation rather than costly conditioning-correction estimation.

**Background**: Doob's h-transform is a stochastic-process technique that transforms a Markov process into a new one with desired properties, such as conditioning on hitting a specific point; for Itô diffusions the transformed process gains an explicit drift term depending on ∇log h. Diffusion models generate data by iteratively denoising noise, and fine-tuning them with reinforcement learning to maximize a reward is often framed as a Markov decision process, as in methods like DDPO. Classifier-free guidance is a widely used technique that trades off sample quality and diversity by combining conditional and unconditional predictions, and this paper recasts such guidance through the same h-transform lens.

The paper introduces scTrilemma, a latent-bottleneck variational autoencoder that routes expression-derived variation to the embedding, the decoder, or the prior instead of forcing all variation through a single embedding. The method uses a single reconstruction objective with no target annotations or auxiliary representation losses, and latent interventions show that context can be removed at almost no cost to the other demands, leaving identity versus fidelity as the remaining tension. ## [AC2 Uses Learned Critics to Skip Full Rollouts in LLM RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39247) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Actor-Critic with Action Chunking (AC2), a method that assigns credit to action chunks of roughly 10k tokens using a learned critic, removing the need to roll every trajectory to completion. Trained on Qwen3-4B with FineProofs-RL and evaluated on IMO-ProofBench, AC2 surpasses GRPO's peak validation score of 18.5% using 2.5x fewer decoding FLOPs and 25% fewer training steps. This challenges the common assumption that learned critics are too inaccurate to trust for LLM reinforcement learning, where critics have typically been used only for baseline estimation. By enabling policy updates without terminal rewards, AC2 opens a previously unexplored design space for more efficient LLM RL algorithms. AC2 makes critic-based credit assignment reliable through three design choices: local readiness, which applies critic-based updates only when the critic is sufficiently accurate on a given problem; providing the critic with a reference solution from a previous successful rollout when available; and assigning credit over action chunks of 10k tokens rather than individual tokens. The reported gains come from needing 25% fewer training steps and generating fewer tokens per step, since the policy does not need to continue every trajectory to completion.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Reinforcement learning for large language models typically relies on sparse, outcome-level rewards, which makes credit assignment difficult: standard algorithms assign the same terminal advantage to every token in a long rollout. Actor-critic methods can provide finer-grained credit assignment, but learned critics are generally considered too inaccurate to trust when training LLMs, so even when a critic is present it is used only for baseline estimation. Action chunking, grouping multiple actions into a single decision unit, has been explored in robotics and offline-to-online RL as a way to improve TD-based actor-critic algorithms.

## [Fenchel Tilt Flow Control Enables Efficient Generative Model Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.40030) ⭐️ 7.0/10

The paper introduces Fenchel Tilt Flow Control (FTFC), a method that decouples utility optimization from generative-model fitting by jointly fitting an effective reward and density-ratio weights on pretrained samples using Fenchel duality and f-divergence penalties. These frozen weights then modify a diffusion or flow model in a single stage of importance-weighted denoising or flow matching, achieving up to 20× greater efficiency and improved performance across image and molecule generation benchmarks. This work addresses a key trade-off in reward alignment for generative models: existing finetuning methods either restrict the family of supported preferences or sacrifice efficiency for generality. FTFC offers a general and computationally efficient approach that could make preference alignment more practical for diverse applications such as guided design and constraint satisfaction. FTFC establishes exact duality for concave utilities under suitable conditions and shows that weighted fitting reproduces the optimal target distribution for a given utility. The method supports general f-divergence penalties that determine how rewards are transformed into distribution-correction weights, and it avoids differentiating through sampling trajectories.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Generative models such as diffusion models learn to produce data by reversing a noise-adding process, and adapting them to specific preferences (e.g., generating images with certain attributes) typically requires finetuning. Fenchel duality is a mathematical result in convex analysis that relates a convex function's optimization to its conjugate, while f-divergence is a family of measures (including KL divergence) that quantifies differences between probability distributions. FTFC combines these tools to efficiently steer pretrained generative models toward arbitrary utility functions without costly retraining.

ComputerSD introduces an online self-distillation method for computer-use agents (CUAs) that converts real-time feedback from executed GUI transitions into token-level guidance and step-level value scores, jointly optimizing on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) and trajectory-level GRPO in a fully asynchronous training framework. On OSWorld-Verified, it outperforms outcome-only GRPO by 1.9 and 4.1 percentage points on the general-purpose Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking and specialized EvoCUA-8B backbones, respectively. Existing CUA online training relies mainly on sparse outcome rewards that give no supervision for intermediate actions, so this work shows how dense, real-time GUI feedback can be turned into usable learning signals. If it generalizes, it could improve GUI automation agents that must operate browsers and desktop applications through screenshots and clicks, an area of active interest from OpenAI's Operator to Microsoft Copilot Studio. A fine-tuned GUI analyzer produces guidance and a step-level value score after each action; the guidance supplies privileged context while the score regulates the resulting OPSD signals, addressing the misalignment of fixed guidance with the student's current state and conflicts between guidance-induced probability shifts and step-level correctness. Evaluation in out-of-distribution settings further supports generalizability, though the work is an arXiv preprint without community discussion yet.

On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a training technique in which a model samples its own trajectories while a privileged self-teacher provides dense token-level supervision, avoiding the distribution mismatch of off-policy distillation. ## [Causal World Models for Modular LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00012) ⭐️ 6.0/10

This paper introduces FedCausalCompose, a causal world-model framework for modular LLM agents that uses intervention-response evidence to improve cross-module planning over observational models. It shows that observational world models incur an irreducible interventional error under unblocked back-door paths, and that causal interfaces help most in structured tool environments where API signatures expose preconditions and downstream effects. This work addresses a non-trivial gap in LLM agent planning by highlighting the limitations of observational world models and proposing a causal framework that could influence future research on modular agent architectures. It identifies a concrete condition for when causal structure helps: cross-module interfaces must be both statistically identifiable and presented in a form the agent can use at action time. The paper provides theoretical insights including irreducible interventional error, coverage benefits, and the conditions under which an oracle causal composition can beat the non-causal lower bound. It also notes that dialogue and narrative environments often ignore raw edge lists unless a short attention anchor makes the causal information decision-relevant.

**Background**: World models in LLM agents are typically fit to observational traces, but this is not the quantity needed for intervention-time planning: a trace may show that payment precedes shipment without identifying whether payment authorizes shipment, inventory mediates the effect, or a hidden trigger explains both. Causal inference concepts such as back-door paths and intervention-response evidence are used to address this gap. Modular systems like order, payment, inventory, and shipment services are common in LLM agent applications, where actions in one module change which transitions are valid in another.

A new arXiv paper (2610.00437) introduces JevSpawn, a compositional policy that connects natural language task specifications to finite probabilistic exploration for LLM agents. It couples parallel action spawning with feedback-driven branch selection, representation revision, and recovery from retained alternatives, and was evaluated on eight benchmark tasks against seven agent baselines plus a TypeSafe Jev variant. LLM agents currently generate reasoning and actions token by token, making long interactions slow and expensive; JevSpawn's approach could make agentic inference faster and more adaptive without additional training. If validated, it could influence how autonomous agents derive and revise their action spaces from natural language instructions. JevSpawn relies on shared action structure and model prefixes to reduce repeated generation and context computation, and it requires no additional training. However, the work is an arXiv preprint without peer review or released code, so its reported improvements over seven baselines remain to be independently verified.

JevSpawn addresses this gap by composing natural language specifications with finite probabilistic exploration, building on prior work in compositional policies that translate language instructions into combinations of pretrained policies.

A new arXiv paper (2610.00529) introduces the Ontology-Based Contextual AI Evaluation (OB-CAIE) methodology, which uses two ontologies — a Domain-Specific Ontology (DSO) and an Evaluation Process Ontology (EPO) — to define what will be tested and how. The DSO captures the 'what' of the problem space, while the EPO captures the 'how', together forming a canonical, traceable evaluation problem space. AI evaluation often suffers from unclear testing coverage, poor reproducibility, and an ad-hoc balance between human judgment and automation. OB-CAIE aims to bring scientific rigor to these evaluations by making failure points traceable and visualizable, which could benefit AI evaluation researchers, benchmark designers, and organizations deploying AI in complex domains. The methodology explicitly allows human judgment at specific, scientifically grounded points, particularly in complex subject areas where human feedback is genuinely irreducible or machine irreplaceable. A key claimed advantage is that failure points can be traced, visualized, and analyzed within the canonical OB-CAIE problem space, though the paper presents no empirical results yet.

OB-CAIE builds on this idea by separating domain knowledge (DSO) from evaluation process knowledge (EPO), so that evaluations can be designed, repeated, and audited more systematically.

## [New Doxastic Deontic Logic Reduces Norm-Guided Decisions to MaxSAT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00668) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv preprint (2610.00668) introduces a doxastic deontic logic that combines a classically reducible fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic with multi-agent KD45, adding explicit conditional norms so that norms can depend on agents' beliefs about both facts and norms. The authors define a Doxastic Norm Compliance Optimization Problem and prove conditions under which subjective and objective optimization coincide and optimal decision-making reduces to weighted partial MaxSAT in polynomial time. Autonomous systems often must act under conflicting norms and incomplete or unreliable information, so a logic that formally links beliefs, norms, and decisions could make norm-aware agents more principled and verifiable. The polynomial-time reduction to weighted partial MaxSAT also suggests that mature SAT/MaxSAT solvers could be reused for practical norm-guided decision making. The logic is built on a classically reducible fragment of Chellas' Minimal Deontic Logic and multi-agent KD45, where KD45 is the standard modal logic of belief. The paper distinguishes subjective optimization relative to an agent's beliefs from objective optimization relative to actual facts, and gives conditions under which the two coincide; the reduction to weighted partial MaxSAT is polynomial.

## [OSCAR Framework Routes LLMs to Verify Optimization Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00912) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduced OSCAR (Optimization modeling by Simulator, Coder, And Reviewer), a framework that uses an offline certified simulator to verify and improve LLM-generated optimization models by sequentially routing queries to different LLMs based on cost and capability. On five benchmark problems, OSCAR achieved 95% to 100% accuracy using two small open-weight LLMs, each deployable locally on a single GPU, while Codex and Claude Code incurred average token costs 3.1 and 5.8 times higher, respectively. This work addresses a practical risk in using LLMs for operations research: executable code may misrepresent constraints or objectives, so a solver can return an optimal solution to the wrong problem. By combining certified simulation with cost-aware LLM routing, OSCAR offers organizations a lower-cost, locally deployable way to produce accurate optimization formulations, which matters as LLM capabilities and prices keep changing. OSCAR models the search for the next certified improvement as sequential decisions under unobserved difficulty, giving conditions under which cost-ordered escalation is optimal in a simplified known-prior setting and a prior-free competitive guarantee for general menus. The two small open-weight LLMs had single-attempt accuracies averaging 29% and 48%, and OSCAR supports open-weight models locally or in the cloud depending on budget and confidentiality requirements.

The deterministic ABDA engine remains the sole source of arguments, attacks, and acceptance labels, and every LLM proposal is validated and must be confirmed by the user before taking effect. The system builds on ASPIC+ with strict and defeasible rules, strong negation, defeasible assumptions, and rule preferences, and supports what-if exploration by suspending assumptions and rules or changing preferences.

ProtoFlow introduces a prototype-guided flow matching framework for multivariate time series forecasting that replaces the generic Gaussian prior with a structured prior built from a trained VQ codebook. It combines vector-quantized autoencoding with a DiT-based rectified flow to transport samples from learned latent prototypes to future representations conditioned on historical observations. Existing VQ-based forecasting methods rely on autoregressive token generation, which suffers from exposure bias and training-inference mismatch, while diffusion-based approaches require many sampling steps at inference. ProtoFlow's non-autoregressive design avoids rollout mismatch and enables efficient inference, potentially offering a more practical generative forecasting approach for high-dimensional time series. The method first maps multivariate sequences into a discrete latent space via vector quantization, then constructs a structured prior from the learned codebook, and finally learns a DiT-based rectified flow to transport samples from this prior to future latent representations. Experiments on benchmark datasets reportedly show consistently superior forecasting performance with efficient inference and faster training convergence.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Multivariate time series forecasting predicts future values across multiple correlated variables, and generative models such as diffusion have shown strong promise but are slow because they need many iterative sampling steps. Vector quantization (VQ) compresses continuous data into a compact set of discrete codebook entries, enabling controllable latent-space modeling, but existing VQ forecasting methods generate tokens autoregressively, which causes exposure bias. Flow matching is a simulation-free generative modeling technique that learns a vector field transporting a simple prior distribution to the data distribution, and ProtoFlow's key insight is that the trained VQ codebook already captures representative latent prototypes that can serve as a more informative prior than generic Gaussian noise.

## [Paper Proposes Generation-Provenance Substrate for Auditing Synthetic Speech](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01378) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01378) proposes a 'generation-provenance substrate' that binds a synthetic research object's source specification, generated content, waveform, target, fact requirements, quality signals, review lineage, and immutable manifest identity. The authors demonstrate the substrate in a private Japanese care-handoff pipeline audit covering a 113-asset review population with 1.552 hours of synthetic speech across six scenario families. The work addresses a critical gap in AI reproducibility: attributing model behavior to synthetic training data requires knowing what produced each item before estimating what it caused, yet waveform-label pairs alone do not preserve this knowledge. It offers a compact provenance contract and audit protocol that could inform how synthetic-data pipelines are documented and audited across speech and other generative domains. All 113 items have linked audio, transcripts, candidate notes, and fact checklists, but human evidence is selective and source-specific; two faithful-only manifests are scenario-seed-disjoint and immutably versioned. Exact upstream attribution remains blocked by floating generator aliases, missing per-clip TTS and code stamps, and an unversioned checking prompt, and the authors explicitly do not claim causal training-data attribution, clinical validity, or unrestricted public release.

**Background**: Synthetic data provenance records how a dataset was generated, what parameters were used, and how outputs connect to downstream artifacts, going beyond traditional real-world data provenance. In speech synthesis, research objects are typically stored as waveform-label pairs that lose generation context, making it hard to trace which generator, prompt, or pipeline produced a given clip. This paper argues that generation provenance is necessary but not sufficient for behavior attribution, since it defines the candidate causal graph and audit units while contributive attribution still requires frozen training runs and intervention or influence evidence.

## [DRelay uses global draft context to repair parallel speculative decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01439) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01439) proposes DRelay, a method that uses global information from an entire draft block to perform prefix-aware selective repair of candidate selections before target-model verification. On eight benchmarks with an H800 GPU, DRelay improves average acceptance length and end-to-end decoding speed over DFlash, Domino, and DSpark, achieving 14.7%-16.8%, 8.7%-9.3%, and 8.1%-9.3% speedups respectively under SGLang serving. Speculative decoding is a key technique for accelerating LLM inference without sacrificing output quality, but parallel drafting suffers from early selection errors that truncate the accepted prefix. DRelay's repair mechanism directly addresses this bottleneck, potentially making parallel speculative decoding more effective for latency-sensitive LLM serving. DRelay uses a global reader to extract predictive information across positions for each candidate, and a causal selector that combines candidate-level information with tokens selected at preceding positions to decide whether to retain or replace the native choice. The draft backbone and selector are jointly trained with a repair objective weighted by each block position's potential contribution to the consecutive accepted prefix.

**Background**: Speculative decoding pairs a large target model with a lightweight draft mechanism that proposes multiple tokens per forward pass, which the target model then verifies in parallel. Parallel drafting reduces drafting overhead but its speedup is limited by the accepted prefix length: a single early selection error can prevent all subsequent correct predictions from being used. DRelay introduces a repair step before verification to fix such early errors and extend the accepted prefix.

## [Routing Entropy Fails as Uncertainty Signal in Attention-Residual Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01495) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.01495) audits whether routing entropy in Attention-Residual (AR) variants of Swin-Tiny and DeiT-Small carries information about prediction correctness beyond the model's own confidence. Training from scratch on CIFAR-10/100 with a soft-binned calibration auxiliary loss, the authors find that no test in a fixed 30-test binned family survives multiplicity correction, and across 24 paired runs a scalar routing probe yields no pooled improvement in routing-stratified calibration. This rigorous negative result cautions researchers against treating diffuse routing traces as a free uncertainty signal in dynamic architectures, and it provides a methodological template—multiplicity correction, seed replication, and sensitivity audits—for evaluating claimed internal uncertainty signals. It is most relevant to those working on uncertainty quantification, dynamic/sparse architectures, and model calibration. The audit includes a sensitivity check showing that at an injected effect of 0.010 nats the entropy-profile probe recovers only 24–59% of the oracle gain, while a reference-preserving correction probe recovers just 8% and 23% in the two CIFAR-100 settings—below the threshold the authors fixed for applying it to real labels. The authors emphasize that the results establish control-dependent gains and incomplete estimator recovery, not the absence of conditional routing information.

**Background**: Attention-Residual Transformers replace standard fixed-weight residual connections with learned, input-dependent attention over preceding layer outputs, producing a per-example routing trace alongside each prediction. ## [CoEvolve Separates Construction and Editing for Visual Grounding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.01710) ⭐️ 6.0/10

CoEvolve introduces a construct-to-edit framework for visual grounding that splits the task into explicit state construction and state editing, using Region-Evolution Reinforcement (RER) to build a progressive semantic-spatial trajectory and a Bidirectional Denoising Refiner (BDR) to refine coordinate fields. With a 9B backbone, it rivals models up to 241B parameters, and a single BDR pass improves mean box overlap by over 27 percentage points under controlled corruption. Most multimodal grounding models collapse target identification, spatial reasoning, and boundary estimation into a single terminal prediction, making intermediate localization errors hard to diagnose or correct. By exposing measurable, editable spatial states, CoEvolve offers a more interpretable and correctable path to grounding, which matters for vision-language researchers and applications like remote sensing and image understanding. The framework uses geometry- and behavior-level objectives to consolidate reliable candidates, preserve accurate inputs, or correct toward annotations, and evaluations cover both natural-image and remote-sensing grounding. State-source comparisons support the complementarity of explicit state construction and source-matched editing, though the work is a preprint without peer review.

**Background**: Visual grounding is the multimodal task of localizing an image region that corresponds to a natural language description, typically by outputting a bounding box. Traditional grounding models often produce free-form rationales that make reasoning linguistically explicit but do not expose measurable, editable spatial states, so intermediate errors can persist in the final box. CoEvolve addresses this by separating grounding into explicit state construction and state editing, drawing on reinforcement learning for region evolution and bidirectional denoising for coordinate refinement.

The study uses a natural language inference setup over the Medical Abstracts corpus with five enriched hypotheses per diagnostic category and a balanced sample of 1,000 texts per class. The work directly tackles the disagreement problem in Explainable AI, where different attribution methods give divergent explanations for the same prediction, which undermines trust in model auditing. The framework standardizes explanations through top-token attribution and finds that high predictive accuracy holds in well-defined clinical domains but degrades under high semantic ambiguity, with explanatory convergence strong in univalent categories and dropping sharply under diagnostic uncertainty. A new arXiv paper proposes SW-KAN, a Kolmogorov-Arnold Network variant that replaces bounded polynomial bases with Stieltjes-Wigert q-orthogonal polynomials defined on the semi-infinite domain (0, infinity). It introduces a smooth exponential-of-tanh mapping to bridge unbounded inputs to this domain while preserving well-conditioned gradients, and uses a numerically stable three-term recurrence that evaluates expansions in O(N) operations without special-function calls. Polynomial-based KAN variants have improved on the original B-spline implementation's computational overhead, but they inherit a fundamental domain mismatch between unbounded real-valued inputs and bounded orthogonal polynomial supports. SW-KAN directly targets this underexplored issue and reports better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs, which could make KANs more practical for resource-constrained settings such as reduced feature dimensionality and limited training data. The architecture relies on the log-normal weight structure and a learnable q-parameter of Stieltjes-Wigert polynomials, which together provide a distinct inductive bias for robust performance under constrained resources. Experiments span image classification and continuous function approximation, where SW-KAN reportedly outperforms established polynomial KAN baselines and approximates complex multivariate functions with remarkably few parameters.

**Background**: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) are a neural architecture inspired by the Kolmogorov-Arnold representation theorem; instead of fixed activation functions and linear weights like MLPs, KANs place learnable univariate functions on the edges, often represented with splines. Stieltjes-Wigert polynomials are a family of basic hypergeometric orthogonal polynomials in the basic Askey scheme, defined with respect to a log-normal weight on the semi-infinite domain. Because such polynomial bases are only well-behaved on bounded or semi-infinite supports, feeding unbounded real-valued inputs into them creates a domain mismatch that must be handled by a suitable input mapping.

A new arXiv study evaluated six language-model configurations on 1,200 requests for six distinct random integers from 1-49 using four English prompt variants, with 1,184 valid tickets produced. Effective diversity of number frequencies ranged from only 9.9 to 18.0, far below the simulated fifth-percentile threshold of 46.6-46.7 expected under independent uniform six-of-49 sampling, and modal tickets accounted for 22.5-68.0% of valid responses. A reanalysis of a PNAS 2025 study by Laurito et al. rebuilt the three 5x5 generator-by-selector matrices from 21,828 valid trials and found no statistically significant own-model premium: +0.013 for products (p=0.24), -0.010 for paper abstracts (p=0.74), +0.054 for films (p=0.07), and +0.019 pooled (p=0.14). The original finding that models share a taste for model-written text remains intact, with GPT-4's descriptions chosen 77% to 95% of the time. This work clarifies that the widely discussed "AI-AI bias" is a shared preference for model-written text rather than a self-recognition effect, which matters for how we interpret LLM-as-a-judge evaluations and for designing fair benchmarks. It also demonstrates the value of rigorous replication and reanalysis in AI research, where headline effects can mask more nuanced statistical realities. The analysis used a two-way fixed-effects model with an own-model term gamma, tested via exact permutation over 120 relabellings; the design had 82% power to detect a 0.05 premium for products, 88% for papers, 42% for films, and 97% pooled, with a minimum detectable effect of 0.034 pooled at 80% power. Position bias moved single cells by up to 0.42 share points, but removing order-driven items left the own-model contrast unchanged, and the 4x4 matrix from Tan et al. (ACL 2024) gave a larger gamma of +0.148.

A new arXiv paper (2610.00374) proposes Frame-Evidence Co-Adaptation (FECA), a framework that generates charts in multimodal deep research by iteratively adapting visual frames to the evidence actually retrieved from the web. Instead of fixing a chart plan first and verifying it afterward, FECA lets each frame guide evidence acquisition while the retrieved evidence decides whether that frame is accepted, revised, or dropped before rendering. Analytical charts encode quantitative claims, so unfaithful values can mislead readers of AI-generated research reports; FECA shifts chart generation from post-hoc verification to evidence-grounded visual reasoning, which could improve trustworthiness in deep research systems and fact-checking pipelines. The method is inspired by the bidirectional sensemaking process in Data-Frame Theory, modeling chart generation as an iterative interaction between visual frames and retrieved evidence. The core problem it targets is that predefined visualization plans may demand entities, temporal ranges, or comparison dimensions that retrieved evidence only partially supports, and existing post-hoc verification can flag unsupported values but cannot change the underlying visual frame.

FAER introduces an auditable full-trajectory replay framework with a learner-aware utility selector (FAER-UTILITY) that is fitted on disjoint calibration blocks and uses a disposable optimizer-aware virtual update to build a magnitude-aware utility surface.
