This matters for practitioners who build replay-based post-training pipelines, because it suggests that how cached trajectories are ranked can be as important as the training algorithm itself, and it provides an audit contract that freezes observed fields and replay traces before evaluation labels are joined. The audit contract freezes observed fields and replay traces before evaluation labels are joined, and the metadata-only cross-fitted calibration reaches 0.6476±0.0139 over eight seeds (median 0.6481; paired 95% interval [+0.079,+0.122]) at 63,276 target-run tokens, with a recorded full cost of 189,642 tokens and 3.48 GPU-hours including calibration. Notably, format-feedback selects records with correctness 0.6953 versus 0.3594 for the fixed selector, yet produces a different downstream ranking, illustrating that cache-level correctness and learner utility are distinct objectives.

## [MatrixReward Builds Rewards from Rubric Win-Rate Matrices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00389) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper proposes MatrixReward, a reward mechanism that builds rewards from a rollout-by-rubric win-rate matrix, comparing every pair of sampled responses under each rubric. Evaluated with Qwen3-8B on four open-ended query-answering benchmarks, it achieves an average score of 63.02, outperforming the strongest baseline by roughly 2.0%. Open-ended generation lacks standard answers, so reward design is a central bottleneck for RLHF and reinforcement learning on generative models. MatrixReward shows that relative comparisons organized into a matrix can yield more informative rewards than pointwise rubric scores, which could influence how future reward models and rubric-based evaluation pipelines are built. The method derives data-dependent rubric weights from two statistics: the spread of each matrix column, which captures how strongly a rubric distinguishes current rollouts, and correlations between columns, which reveal rubric repetition; these are combined with prior rubric weights. After column normalization and weighting, per-rubric maxima and minima define positive and negative ideal profiles, and each rollout's distance to these ideals determines its relative-closeness quality reward.

For open-ended tasks where no single correct answer exists, pointwise scoring rubrics are often used, but merging multiple rubric judgments into one score can hide differences between candidate answers. MatrixReward instead uses pairwise win-rate comparisons across rubrics to construct a richer reward signal.

A new arXiv paper (2610.00424) quantifies the gap between the potential gain of a causal predictor and the gain actually realized by a trained repair in a scalar Gaussian causal experiment with known intervention geometry. It derives a sharp leading-log frontier for the assessment exponent, showing it equals min{ℓ_k, 2kη_k/U} to first relative order, and proposes a diagnostic-abstention rule that attains this exponent even with unknown nuisance parameters. This work clarifies that knowing how much a causal predictor could improve does not reveal how much a learned repair actually improves, isolating how the assessment target changes information requirements. At the usual 1/k learning scale, every feasible learner incurs a k^{-2} assessment floor even when oracle potential is estimable at a faster rate; the frontier is characterized in the magnitude-rich regime with ℓ_k = log(1/(k^2 E_k)), where E_k is auxiliary precision. The paper also bounds the critical allowance window, transfers the frontier to adaptive sampling via exact Gaussian simulation, and notes the result is not a general causal identifiability claim.

## [TS-Router Uses Pretrained Representations to Route Anomaly Detectors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00978) ⭐️ 6.0/10

TS-Router proposes a generalist-representation, specialist-detection framework that uses pretrained temporal representations to estimate the relative competence of heterogeneous anomaly detectors and select suitable specialists for each target time series. It derives soft competence supervision from specialists' relative performance on labeled simulated tasks, avoiding the need for specialist-performance labels from real tasks, and requires no target anomaly labels at deployment. Time-series anomaly detection struggles to generalize across datasets because different temporal dynamics imply different notions of normality and favor different detection criteria. By using foundation-model representations to coordinate specialized detectors rather than imposing a universal scoring mechanism, TS-Router offers a promising path toward more adaptable and transferable anomaly detection systems. The framework bounds Top-k set-competence regret under representation coverage and conditional competence stability, and only the selected specialists are fitted unsupervisedly on the target series. Across 16 real-world benchmarks and four complementary evaluation metrics, TS-Router achieves the best overall average rank, with controlled ablations using multiple frozen TSFM encoders supporting the use of pretrained representations for competence estimation.

## [MSE Reconstruction Loss Causes Optimization Imbalance in LLM Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00983) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2610.00983) systematically studies how the reconstruction loss scale affects optimization in sequential learning-based post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models. The authors uncover an "Optimization Imbalance": reconstruction loss magnitudes vary dramatically across quantization stages under MSE, producing highly uneven gradient magnitudes and parameter updates, and they show that RMSE variants at the sample, channel, token, and element levels act as a drop-in replacement that implicitly normalizes gradients and significantly outperforms MSE. This work identifies a simple but previously overlooked design flaw in the loss function used by many state-of-the-art learning-based PTQ methods, and offers a drop-in fix that could improve quantized LLM accuracy without changing the overall pipeline. It matters for researchers and engineers deploying LLMs under tight memory and compute budgets, since better PTQ directly translates into cheaper inference with less accuracy loss. The study spans representative learning-based PTQ methods, multiple LLM families, model scales, architectures, quantization settings, and tasks, consistently reproducing the imbalance. The authors theoretically show that RMSE variants defined at the sample, channel, token, and element levels realize the principle of decoupling optimization strength from reconstruction loss scale through implicit gradient normalization.

A new arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.01028) introduces POTER, a reweighting framework based on optimal transport that assigns sample importance by measuring the transport geometry between the training distribution and a reference distribution built from limited validation group annotations. Spurious correlations and label noise are two of the most common causes of real-world model failure, yet their intersection has been largely underexplored. By decoupling sample importance from loss signals, POTER offers a more robust reweighting strategy that could improve reliability in high-stakes domains such as medical imaging and autonomous driving where minority subgroups and noisy annotations are prevalent. POTER derives sample importance from optimal transport geometry rather than loss values, which prevents mislabeled samples with large losses from contaminating the reweighting process. It relies on a reference distribution constructed from limited validation group annotations and avoids the retraining paradigm common in recent robust learning work, though its dependence on group annotations may limit applicability when such labels are unavailable.

Researchers propose the Mutual Correlation Impact Ratio Method (MCIR-M), a dependence-aware global feature-importance approach that quantifies the unique predictive information each feature contributes beyond its strongly dependent neighbors. The population MCIR score lies in [0,1] and equals zero under exact conditional redundancy, providing a theoretical reliability guarantee. ## [FERPO: Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization for Continuous Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02198) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers propose Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization (FERPO), an on-policy maximum entropy RL algorithm that improves policies using critic values without differentiating the critic with respect to actions. FERPO derives an optimal target action distribution from an entropy- and KL-regularized policy-improvement objective, then fits the actor to this target by minimizing a forward-KL objective estimated via self-normalized importance sampling (SNIS). Many state-of-the-art continuous-control RL methods update policies using action gradients of a learned critic, but critics are trained to predict returns, and accurate value predictions do not guarantee accurate action derivatives, which can cause unreliable policy updates. By avoiding critic differentiation, FERPO offers a more stable policy-improvement path and reports competitive performance and sample-efficiency gains on MuJoCo Playground and ManiSkill. FERPO uses forward KL rather than reverse KL: reverse-KL objectives can favor a subset of the target distribution's modes, while the forward-KL objective encourages coverage of multiple high-value modes and thereby promotes exploration. The KL regularization limits the target distribution's deviation from the rollout policy, keeping the importance weights well behaved, and computational benchmarks show faster actor updates than Relative Entropy Pathwise Policy Optimization (REPPO).

An arXiv paper (2603.19042v5) proposes a conceptual framework that organizes the fragmented literature on AI in judicial decision making into three central questions: the predictive validity of automated risk assessment tools, how algorithmic risk assessments compare with human predictions (AI-versus-Human), and how algorithmic recommendations affect judges' decisions (AI-plus-Human). Using criminal justice risk assessment as a focal case, the authors synthesize empirical evidence and find that AI decision aids have so far had at most modest effects on pretrial and sentencing decisions. This framework helps researchers, legal practitioners, and policymakers in AI ethics, law, and policy navigate a fragmented body of work and identify what is actually known versus assumed about AI in courts. It highlights substantial gaps in understanding how judges respond to AI advice, which is critical as risk assessment tools become more widely deployed in criminal justice systems. The review identifies important limitations in existing research on predictive validity and substantial gaps in understanding how judges respond to AI advice and how those responses vary across individuals and decision-making environments. The authors conclude that further research is needed to understand how judges make decisions in noisy informational environments and under what conditions AI tools can produce meaningful improvements.

**Background**: Predictive validity refers to the ability of a test or measurement method to predict a future outcome, such as whether a defendant will reoffend. Criminal justice risk assessment tools, which have been used since the 1920s but have accelerated in recent years, compile data like crime history and housing information to assign risk scores used in bail, sentencing, and parole decisions. Algorithmic fairness concerns arise because machine learning models trained on historical data can reproduce or amplify biases related to sensitive variables like race or gender.

## [Spatial Atlas: Compute-Grounded Reasoning for Spatial AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12102) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Spatial Atlas introduces compute-grounded reasoning (CGR), a design pattern where code deterministically computes answerable sub-problems from explicit intermediate representations before a language model generates an answer. It is implemented as an Agent2Agent (A2A) server with a spatial question-answering handler and an ML-engineering handler, plus a benchmark driver that enforces strict metric evaluation. This approach could improve the reliability and interpretability of spatial-aware AI agents by ensuring that quantitative sub-problems are solved deterministically rather than estimated by a language model. It also offers a reusable design pattern for building agent systems that need verifiable, evidence-grounded reasoning. The spatial handler extracts a scene graph via a language model, then code fills in missing distances and checks safety rules; the benchmark bridge computes horizontal gaps from segmentation masks and a reconstructed point map, returns a fixed unavailable answer when evidence checks fail, and never falls back to model-estimated coordinates. The ML-engineering handler generates pipeline code and caps repair/refinement passes, but code execution is off by default, and the authors report only one private label-free operational run with no performance or benchmark results.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Spatial reasoning is a challenging capability for AI agents because it requires understanding distances, layouts, and safety constraints from visual or geometric data. Compute-grounded reasoning proposes that deterministic code should handle computable sub-problems, leaving the language model to handle only what cannot be computed. Agent2Agent (A2A) is an open protocol that lets different AI agents communicate and collaborate, and scene graphs are structured representations of objects and their spatial relationships.

## [IRFE-ECG Separates Expert Retention from Source Inference in Continual ECG Deployment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.01674) ⭐️ 6.0/10

The paper introduces IRFE-ECG, a controlled continual-deployment framework built on frozen 1024-dimensional ECGFounder features, where each arriving source adds an isolated Balanced-Softmax linear expert and a lightweight router is re-fitted using retained frozen training features and source labels. Across CPSC, PTB-XL, Georgia, and Chapman-Shaoxing, source-aware expert selection reaches 0.7915 ± 0.0036 Macro-F1, while an MLP router without source IDs reaches 0.7756 ± 0.0027 and top-2 margin fusion reaches 0.7782 ± 0.0022, leaving a persistent top-2-to-oracle gap of 0.0111–0.0133 across three domain orders. This work quantifies the deployment gap between knowing the source and autonomously inferring it in continual ECG learning, which is critical for real-world medical AI systems where source metadata may be unavailable. It provides a controlled benchmark and publicly available code, helping the medical AI community understand the limits of source-unknown inference without raw data replay. The method is raw-ECG-replay-free but not memory-free, as it retains frozen feature vectors for router updates; results are record-level because reliable patient identifiers were unavailable, and the top-2 improvement over the MLP router is small (+0.0026) and not statistically significant under paired bootstrap.

## [IQACO Hybrid Method Combines Implicit Q-Learning with Ant Colony Optimization for Satellite Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24471) ⭐️ 6.0/10

A new arXiv paper (2608.24471v2) proposes IQACO, a hybrid method that embeds an offline implicit Q-learning (IQL) module into constructive ant colony optimization (ACO) to adaptively tune the pheromone factor, heuristic factor, and evaporation rate for maritime moving-target observation scheduling with agile Earth observation satellites. Experiments across 14 scenarios show IQACO improves the mean objective value over conventional ACO by 2.86%–9.41%. This work demonstrates that offline value learning can serve as an effective adaptive search-control mechanism for constrained combinatorial optimization, potentially offering a general template for hybridizing reinforcement learning with metaheuristics in dynamic scheduling domains. It is relevant to researchers in satellite mission planning, RL, and combinatorial optimization, though the application remains niche. Rather than directly learning a task-selection policy, IQACO uses a compact search-state representation capturing pheromone distribution, current and historical-best solution quality, and iteration progress; the learned policy then adjusts ACO's search behavior online. The method was validated on 14 scenarios with varying scales and satellite configurations, and supplementary experiments demonstrated robustness across different scheduling conditions.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Agile Earth observation satellites can slew and point their sensors, making their scheduling a complex combinatorial optimization problem: the scheduler must select targets, assign satellites, choose observation windows, and order observations under time-window, attitude-maneuvering, and onboard-resource constraints. When targets are moving on the sea surface, feasible observation windows shift continuously with target motion and orbital geometry, making the problem dynamic and sequence-dependent. Ant colony optimization is a metaheuristic inspired by ant foraging, where artificial ants construct solutions guided by pheromone trails and heuristic information, with pheromone evaporation preventing premature convergence. Implicit Q-learning (IQL) is an offline reinforcement learning algorithm that learns a value function from a fixed dataset without querying the environment, avoiding distributional shift issues common in offline RL.

## [IBBench-Light: Paired Evaluation Exposes Hidden Instruction-Following Failures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13725) ⭐️ 6.0/10

IBBench-Light introduces a paired evaluation method that tests the same external record under two different uses — executing a procedure versus processing text — across 144 matched pairs per model, with 1,152 archived greedy responses from four quantized instruction models. The paper reports that Qwen succeeds on 132 execute and 109 process prompts but completes only 97 full pairs, and that in a pinned Phi rerun, changing the end-of-sequence (EOS) token set shifted exact paired success from 0/144 to 62/144. This work shows that marginal per-task averages can mask paired failures, meaning a model may look competent on each task type individually while failing when the same input must be handled consistently under both interpretations. It also demonstrates that a seemingly minor generation configuration choice — the EOS token set — can swing exact paired success rates dramatically, which has direct implications for how LLM evaluations are designed, reported, and reproduced. Paired exact-contract accuracy (PECA) requires both members of a pair to satisfy their output contracts, and the benchmark adds 1,722 logged CPU generations to test directive-absent controls, twelve additional semantic bases, within-base wording changes, and generation stopping. The authors also audit literal-target exposure and case normalization, and note that task margins and paired counts must be read together with the stopping policy.

rss · ArXiv ML (cs.AI) · Oct 2, 04:00

**Background**: Instruction-following benchmarks typically score each prompt independently and report average accuracy, which can hide cases where a model handles one interpretation of an input but not another. IBBench-Light instead keeps the external record in the same structural field and only changes the requested use, creating matched pairs that must both succeed. End-of-sequence (EOS) tokens are special tokens that tell a language model when to stop generating; misconfiguring which token IDs count as EOS can cause generations to truncate early or run on, directly affecting whether an output contract is met.

## [Scan-Derived Prototypes Add Little Over Frozen Foundation Features](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04381) ⭐️ 6.0/10

This paper disentangles the contributions of scan-derived geometric prototypes, label supervision, and query protocols in 3D object recognition over frozen foundation features. ## [Triangular Resampling Cuts Long-Horizon Motion Diffusion Error](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34697) ⭐️ 6.0/10

Researchers introduced Triangular Resampling (TR), a post-training method that extends rollout-based training to partially denoised states within the active window of FloodDiffusion's triangular denoising schedule, using ground-truth clamping to limit drift. On 120-second motion generation from HumanML3D test prompts, supervised TR reduced FID AUC by 40.9% and the FID degradation slope by 55.3% compared with matched post-training without replay, and both TR and its distribution-matching variant TR-DMD achieved state-of-the-art FID AUC in their respective comparison groups. Long-horizon error accumulation is a central obstacle for diffusion-based motion generation, where small per-step errors compound over long rollouts and degrade realism. By targeting the mismatch between ground-truth training windows and model-generated inference states, TR offers a practical post-training recipe that could improve streaming and long-duration motion synthesis for researchers and applications in animation, robotics, and virtual agents. For each replayed sample, TR draws a single denoising threshold shared across latent positions and replay updates, replays multi-step triangular denoising without gradient tracking, then replaces states below the threshold with noise-matched ground truth while keeping model predictions at or above it. The same rollout construction supports both supervised training (TR) and distribution matching (TR-DMD), though the abstract reports results only on 120-second HumanML3D generation.
